blocking.title: Stripe payment collection is unconditionally bypassed in production — every order ships free
blocking.proof: stripeSecretKey is bound via `@Value("${STRIPE_SECRET_KEY:}")` (line 53), defaulting to an empty string. I checked where this is actually supplied in production: `docker-compose.prod.yml`'s `server.environment` block (lines 23-42) passes through `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `DEEPSEEK_API_KEY`, and `MINIMAX_API_KEY` explicitly, but contains no `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` or `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET` entry at all — so Compose never forwards these even if an operator sets them in `.env`. `.env.example` also has zero references to either variable (grepped, no hits), and `prod_deploy.sh`'s `setup` step only calls `require_env_vars DB_PASSWORD MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD JWT_SECRET` — it never validates Stripe config. Following the documented `./prod_deploy.sh setup && ./prod_deploy.sh up` flow therefore starts the `server` container with `stripeSecretKey=""` unconditionally. Every `POST /api/checkout` from any authenticated buyer then takes `stubCheckout()` (lines 335-366): it builds an `Order` with `status=PAID`, `paymentStatus="STUB"`, and a fabricated `cs_test_<uuid>` session id — no real Stripe `Session` is ever created and the buyer is never charged — while `analyticsService.record(..., ORDER_PAID, ...)` fires as if payment succeeded. The only signal this happened is an INFO log line ("STRIPE_SECRET_KEY not configured — created stub order..."); nothing surfaces it as a startup warning or health-check failure. Any low-privilege buyer can therefore obtain every item in their cart for free, repeatedly, on the as-shipped production deployment.
blocking.fix: Add `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY: ${STRIPE_SECRET_KEY}` and `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET: ${STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET}` to the `server.environment` block in `docker-compose.prod.yml`, document both as required in `.env.example`, add them to `prod_deploy.sh`'s `require_env_vars` check, and make `CheckoutService` refuse (startup failure or 503 on checkout) rather than silently stub-fulfill when `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod` and the key is blank.
verifierSummary:
[reachable] isReal=true conf=0.95: CONFIRMED — reachable in the as-shipped production configuration; I found no gating, flag, or profile that disables it, and the config half is worse than filed.

Code path: CheckoutService.java:53 binds @Value("${STRIPE_SECRET_KEY:}") (default empty); line 77 does `if (stripeSecretKey == null || stripeSecretKey.isBlank()) return stubCheckout(...)` with no profile/environment check. stubCheckout (~334-366) persists an Order with .status(OrderStatus.PAID), .paymentStatus("STUB"), a fabricated "cs_test_"+UUID session id, fires both CHECKOUT_INITIATED and ORDER_PAID analytics, and returns "/checkout/success?session_id=..." — no stripeGateway.createSession call anywhere on that branch, so the buyer is never charged. Only signal is one INFO log; no startup failure, no health-check surfacing.

Reachability: nginx/conf.d/default.conf lines 27-33 proxy /api/ to the server in the ACTIVE http block (the commented-out block is the HTTPS one). SecurityConfig line 52 is anyRequest().authenticated() and /api/checkout has no stricter matcher or role requirement. CheckoutController is a live @RestController @RequestMapping("/api/checkout") with a @PostMapping; the only additional gate is app.auth.require-email-verification (prod default true), which any buyer self-services. web/app/checkout/page.tsx:102 posts to it and follows the returned url. An authenticated verified buyer is explicitly in scope per the decision rule.

Config: I verified the stronger form of the finding's claim. `grep -rn "env_file" --include="*.yml"` over the repo returns ZERO hits — neither docker-compose.yml nor docker-compose.prod.yml uses env_file, so the container's environment is exactly the explicit `environment:` block (docker-compose.prod.yml lines 23-42), which contains no STRIPE_SECRET_KEY or STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET. Compose's .env is interpolation-only, so an operator CANNOT supply the key via .env or an exported shell var without editing the compose file; the blank key is structurally guaranteed, not merely an operator oversight. Also confirmed: application.yml / application-prod.yml / application-dev.yml contain no stripe property (grep over resources/ hits only V9__checkout_orders.sql's stripe_session_id column); server/Dockerfile declares no ENV/ARG at all; .env.example and the repo's local .env have no Stripe entries; prod_deploy.sh:107 validates only DB_PASSWORD, MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD, JWT_SECRET.

Aggravating factor the finding omits: stubResaleCheckout (~300-321) is the same unconditional bypass on the resale path and additionally calls resaleService.markSold(...), irreversibly consuming a unique pre-loved unit for free. Partial configuration is not a mitigation either: handleWebhook (~line 168) throws IllegalArgumentException("Webhook secret not configured") on a blank STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET, so wiring only the secret key would break fulfillment rather than fix the bypass.

Severity: CRITICAL is right as filed. It is authenticated-buyer reach rather than anonymous, which the rules say does not reduce it, and the harm is silent free fulfillment plus Orders durably marked PAID with ORDER_PAID analytics that are indistinguishable downstream from real revenue — a data-integrity corruption, not just a missing feature. Residual 0.05 uncertainty is only about operator intent (a pre-launch deployment that never means to take money), which does not change the code path or the fabricated PAID records.

[mitigated] isReal=true conf=0.95: I went looking for the mitigating guard under the EXISTING MITIGATION lens and found none at any layer of the stack. Every claim in the finding checked out against the files.

What I read:

1. `server/src/main/java/com/iyae/service/CheckoutService.java:53-54` — `@Value("${STRIPE_SECRET_KEY:}")` with an empty default. Line 77-79: `if (stripeSecretKey == null || stripeSecretKey.isBlank()) return stubCheckout(...)`. `stubCheckout` (335-366) builds `Order` with `status=OrderStatus.PAID`, `paymentStatus="STUB"`, a fabricated `cs_test_<uuid>` id, and fires `analyticsService.record(..., EventType.ORDER_PAID, ...)`. No Stripe `Session` is created. `@PostConstruct initStripe()` (62-67) logs only on the *present* branch — there is not even a warning on absence, just the INFO line at 361.

2. `docker-compose.prod.yml` `server.environment` (lines 22-41) — map form with explicit values; `DB_*`, `JWT_SECRET`, `AI_PROVIDER`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `DEEPSEEK_API_KEY`, `MINIMAX_API_KEY`, `CORS_ORIGINS`, `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: prod`, `FRONTEND_BASE_URL`, `RESEND_MAIL_ENDPOINT`, `INTERNAL_MAIL_SECRET`, `RATE_LIMIT_TRUSTED_PROXIES`. No `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` or `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET`. I specifically grepped for `env_file` in both compose files — zero hits — so Compose has no path to forward an unlisted `.env` value into the container (the map form does not inherit from the host the way a bare `- VAR` list entry would).

3. `prod_deploy.sh` — `COMPOSE_FILE="docker-compose.prod.yml"` (line 4) and every invocation is `docker compose -f "$COMPOSE_FILE"`, a single file, so there is no merge with `docker-compose.yml` (which also lacks the var). `setup` runs `require_env_vars DB_PASSWORD MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD JWT_SECRET` (line 107) — no Stripe validation.

4. `.env.example` — grepped the whole repo for `STRIPE` in `*.yml/*.sh/*.example/Dockerfile*`: the only hits are archived plan docs under `.claude/PRPs/` and `docs/CODEMAPS/dependencies.md`. Nothing in any live config.

5. `application.yml` / `application-prod.yml` — grepped for `stripe`/`checkout`: zero hits. No alternate property source.

6. No fail-closed startup guard: grepped `server/src/main/java` for `@Profile("prod")`, `EnvironmentPostProcessor`, `InitializingBean`, `ApplicationRunner` — zero files.

7. Spring Security is not a guard here: `SecurityConfig` ends at `.anyRequest().authenticated()`; the only additional gate is `CheckoutController`'s `requireEmailVerification` check, which any self-registered buyer clears via the normal self-service verification flow. Email verification is not a payment control.

8. nginx is not a guard: `nginx/conf.d/default.conf` proxies `location /api/` wholesale with no deny/allow on checkout.

9. `/api/health` returns a static `{"status":"UP"}` from `HealthController` — it cannot surface this misconfiguration, matching the finding's claim that nothing escalates it.

Severity stands at CRITICAL: unauthenticated-adjacent (any registered buyer), unconditional on the documented deploy path, silent, and directly financial. I found no partial mitigation to downgrade against.

blocking.title: Path traversal via designer-controlled glbUrl leads to arbitrary file write at startup
blocking.evidence:
String relative = url.substring("/assets/".length());
            Path glbPath = Path.of(assetsOutputDir, relative);
blocking.proof: glbUrl has zero validation: CreateProductRequest.glbUrl / UpdateProductRequest.glbUrl are plain `String` fields with no @Pattern (server/src/main/java/com/iyae/dto/CreateProductRequest.java:33, UpdateProductRequest.java:30), and ProductService.createProduct/updateProduct write it straight onto the entity (ProductService.java:149 `.glbUrl(request.glbUrl())`, line 190-191 `product.setGlbUrl(request.glbUrl())`) with no sanitization. DESIGNER is a self-service role (any registrant can pick it; only ADMIN is blocked per AuthService.java:86-88), and `/api/designer/products` is reachable to any DESIGNER. A malicious designer sets glbUrl="/assets/models/../../../../tmp/pwned.glb" and category="x" on their own product via POST/PUT /api/designer/products. The prefix check `url.startsWith("/assets/models/")` (line 57) does not block ".." segments. On the next application restart (GlbAssetInitializer runs in ALL profiles, including prod, per its own javadoc, and prod_deploy.sh update restarts the server on every deploy), ensureGlbAssets() computes relative="models/../../../../tmp/pwned.glb", builds glbPath outside /var/iyae/assets, finds Files.exists(glbPath) false, and calls GlbPlaceholderGenerator.writeGlbFile(glbPath, category), which does Files.createDirectories(outputPath.getParent()) then Files.write(outputPath, bytes) — creating an attacker-chosen file at an attacker-chosen path. The server container has no USER directive in its Dockerfile (runs as root), and /var/iyae/assets is a volume shared with the worker container, so this is a genuine arbitrary-file-creation primitive reachable by a zero-barrier self-registered account, not just a theoretical path issue.
blocking.fix: Reject (or canonicalize) the path before use: resolve glbPath, call .normalize(), and verify it is still contained in Path.of(assetsOutputDir).normalize() (e.g. glbPath.normalize().startsWith(Path.of(assetsOutputDir).normalize())) before any Files call; also validate CreateProductRequest/UpdateProductRequest.glbUrl server-side (reject any value containing "..", backslashes, or not matching ^/assets/models/[A-Za-z0-9_-]+\.glb$) rather than trusting a free-text field from a self-service role.
verifierSummary: [reachable] isReal=true conf=0.93 sev->HIGH: Could not refute — every link in the chain is present in the production configuration. GlbAssetInitializer is an unconditional @Component/CommandLineRunner (no @Profile, no @ConditionalOnProperty), so it runs under SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod; `grep -rn "normalize()" server/src/main/java` returns zero hits, so nothing canonicalizes the path. Line 57 checks only startsWith("/assets/models/"), which ".." passes; Path.of does not normalize and the OS resolves ".." at open(2), and ensurePlaceholderAssets() runs first so /var/iyae/assets/models exists for resolution. The sink is attacker-fed: CreateProductRequest.glbUrl and UpdateProductRequest.glbUrl are bare Strings with no constraint, ProductService:149 and :190-191 persist them verbatim, findAll() has no status filter (a DRAFT product suffices), and glb_url is VARCHAR(500). The role is self-service: AuthService.register blocks only Role.ADMIN and auto-creates the DesignerProfile for DESIGNER; SecurityConfig:49 gates /api/designer/** on hasRole("DESIGNER") alone. docker-compose.prod.yml leaves worker.output-dir unset for the server (so the /var/iyae/assets default applies), server/Dockerfile has no USER directive (root), assets_data is shared with worker and nginx, and prod_deploy.sh up/update run `docker compose up -d`, firing the runner. Two impact corrections from reading the code: line 62 is `if (!Files.exists(glbPath))`, so this is arbitrary file CREATION, not overwrite (existing jars/configs/authorized_keys cannot be clobbered), and the content is a fixed GLB skeleton whose only attacker-controlled bytes are `category` (VARCHAR(100), with double-quotes stripped at GlbPlaceholderGenerator:48). Also, prod does require email verification before any authenticated access (JwtAuthenticationFilter:57-59 with application-prod.yml keeping the default true), so the attacker needs a working inbox — a nuisance, not a barrier. Realistic impact is therefore root-owned new-file creation inside the server container and the shared assets volume, deferred to the next restart, with a concrete DoS angle (e.g. creating /var/iyae/assets/avatars as a regular file so the worker's makedirs fails) but no demonstrated code-execution chain. Real and blocking; HIGH rather than CRITICAL. The proposed fix (normalize + containment check, plus a DTO pattern on glbUrl) is correct.

[mitigated] isReal=true conf=0.95: REFUTATION FAILED — I looked for a mitigation at every layer named in the lens and found none; I found the opposite.

Verified each link by reading the code:
1. NO Bean Validation: CreateProductRequest.java:33 and UpdateProductRequest.java:30 are bare `String glbUrl` with no @Pattern/@Size. (RegisterRequest.java carries @Pattern/@Size on nearly every field, so validation is plainly in use elsewhere — this field was simply left open.)
2. NO service-layer sanitization: ProductService.java:149 `.glbUrl(request.glbUrl())` and :190-191 `product.setGlbUrl(request.glbUrl())` assign verbatim.
3. NO entity/DB guard: Product.java:59-60 is plain Lombok @Setter, `length = 500`; V1__baseline_schema.sql:54 is `glb_url VARCHAR(500)` — no constraint, and 500 chars is ample for the payload.
4. NO Spring Security barrier of consequence: SecurityConfig gates /api/designer/** on hasRole("DESIGNER"), but AuthService.register:86-88 blocks only Role.ADMIN and RegisterRequest.role is a free `@NotNull Role` — DESIGNER is self-service. I grepped security/ and controller/ for `emailVerified`: zero hits, so there is no verification gate on designer CRUD either (and verification would be self-service anyway).
5. NO profile gate on the sink: GlbAssetInitializer is a plain `@Component @Order(1)` CommandLineRunner with no @Profile/@ConditionalOn — it runs in prod, as its own javadoc states.
6. NO status filter: ensureGlbAssets() iterates productRepository.findAll(), so an unpublished DRAFT product is enough.
7. Container runs as root: server/Dockerfile has no USER directive; ENTRYPOINT is `java -jar app.jar`. docker-compose.prod.yml:43-44 mounts assets_data:/var/iyae/assets (also mounted read-only into nginx at :113, which serves it).

EVIDENCE OF ABSENCE RATHER THAN MITIGATION: GenerationService.sanitizeMediaUrl (lines 243-262) is an explicit `normalized.contains("..")` traversal rejecter written for the sibling designer-controlled `media` field, with the javadoc "so a designer-controlled media entry can't drive the worker into reading arbitrary local files." The same threat model was recognised one field over and glbUrl was missed.

EMPIRICALLY REPRODUCED the exact code pattern in a scratch single-file java program (deleted afterwards; worktree left clean): Path.of(base, "models/../../../../pt_escape/pwned.glb") — Files.exists() returned FALSE (so the `if (!Files.exists(glbPath))` guard at line 62 does NOT block it), Files.createDirectories(parent) succeeded, Files.write created the file OUTSIDE the base directory. `p.normalize().startsWith(Path.of(base).normalize())` returned false, confirming the proposed fix is the correct containment test. Path.of does not normalize; nothing downstream does either.

SEVERITY: left as filed (NONE). Two nuances cut against CRITICAL — the primitive is create-only, not overwrite (line 62's !Files.exists), the content is a mostly-fixed GLB with at most 100 non-quote attacker-controlled chars from `category` (VARCHAR(100)), it is restart-gated, and a stock eclipse-temurin:22-jre container has no cron/sshd/profile.d daemon to convert the write into code execution, so an implied RCE is not demonstrable. Against that, I found an additional vector the finding did not claim: glbUrl="/assets/models/../x.html" lands inside the nginx-served volume, where nginx assigns text/html by extension and the Next.js middleware.ts CSP does not apply — a same-origin stored-XSS primitive needing no escape from the volume at all. Net: a trivially reachable, fully attacker-controlled arbitrary-file-creation-as-root plus a same-origin XSS chain is a legitimate release blocker at the filed severity.

[accurate] isReal=true conf=0.95: Finding confirmed on every factual point; I could not refute any element.

(1) Evidence verbatim: GlbAssetInitializer.java:60-61 is exactly `String relative = url.substring("/assets/".length()); Path glbPath = Path.of(assetsOutputDir, relative);`. I read ensureGlbAssets() in full (lines 52-74): the only guard is line 57 `if (url == null || !url.startsWith("/assets/models/")) continue;` — a prefix test. There is no normalize(), no toRealPath(), no containment check in the class. Path.of does not normalize, so ".." survives to the OS.

(2) Source is unvalidated: CreateProductRequest.java:33 and UpdateProductRequest.java:30 are plain `String glbUrl` with no annotations (both records do use @NotBlank/@DecimalMin/@Valid elsewhere, so validation is active and glbUrl is simply exempt). ProductService.java:149 `.glbUrl(request.glbUrl())` and 190-191 `if (request.glbUrl() != null) product.setGlbUrl(request.glbUrl());` persist it raw. A repo-wide grep for glbUrl found no sanitizer on any write path.

(3) Reachability confirmed: AuthService.register rejects only Role.ADMIN (lines 86-88); RegisterRequest declares `@NotNull Role role`, so DESIGNER is client-chosen and self-service. SecurityConfig:49 gates /api/designer/** to hasRole("DESIGNER"); DesignerProductController has @PostMapping and @PutMapping("/{id}").

(4) Sink confirmed: GlbPlaceholderGenerator.writeGlbFile:93-94 does Files.createDirectories(outputPath.getParent()) then Files.write(outputPath, ...).

(5) Trigger/privilege confirmed: GlbAssetInitializer is an unconditional @Component CommandLineRunner (@Order(1)) with no @Profile and javadoc "Runs in ALL profiles (including production)"; server/Dockerfile has no USER directive (root); docker-compose.yml:46-47 and docker-compose.prod.yml mount assets_data:/var/iyae/assets shared with the worker. No test in server/src/test references GlbAssetInitializer, and server/CLAUDE.md itself lists it under "Untested Areas" — so no test demonstrates the opposite.

Precision note (does not change the verdict, matters for the fix): the Files.write is gated on !Files.exists(glbPath) at line 62, so the primitive is arbitrary file CREATION plus arbitrary directory creation as root — not overwrite of existing files — and the content is a fixed minimal GLB whose only attacker-influenced bytes are the `category` string interpolated into asset.extras with double-quotes stripped (GlbPlaceholderGenerator:48). The finding's text states that precondition correctly ("finds Files.exists(glbPath) false") and does not overclaim overwrite or RCE. Severity left as filed: a traversal-to-filesystem-write primitive reachable by a zero-barrier self-registered role, executing as root into a volume shared with another container, is correctly treated as a release blocker; the create-only and restart-triggered constraints are mitigants but not unreachability. Proposed fix (normalize + containment check, plus a server-side ^/assets/models/[A-Za-z0-9_-]+\.glb$ pattern on both DTOs) is appropriate.

blocking.title: Stale-reservation sweep can release a listing for resale while an earlier buyer's Stripe payment still settles, causing a double-sale with a silent double-charge
blocking.evidence: private static final Duration RESERVATION_TTL = Duration.ofMinutes(30);
blocking.proof: Buyer A clicks Buy Now on a resale listing: reserve() flips it LISTED->RESERVED and a Stripe Checkout Session is created (Stripe's default session lifetime is far longer than 30 minutes, and this code never calls setExpiresAt to shorten it). If Buyer A is slow to pay, or the checkout.session.completed/async_payment_succeeded webhook is delayed past 30 minutes (Stripe's own retry schedule can span hours during an outage), SchedulerConfig.releaseStaleResaleReservations() (fixedDelay=300000) calls ResaleService.releaseStaleReservations(), which unconditionally flips any listing RESERVED past the TTL back to LISTED -- with no check for an in-flight/already-succeeded payment. Buyer B then buys the now-LISTED item and pays (listing -> SOLD). When Buyer A's delayed webhook finally arrives, CheckoutService.fulfillPaidSession (lines 213-240) unconditionally sets Buyer A's order to PAID and calls resaleService.markSold(order.getResaleListingId()) (line 232); ResaleService.markSold (lines 238-244) finds the listing already SOLD, so the UPDATE affects 0 rows and it just logs an INFO line -- no exception, no refund, no flag on the order. Result: Buyer A is charged via Stripe and has an order recorded as PAID for an item that was already shipped to Buyer B, with nothing in the system surfacing the conflict for support/refund.
blocking.fix: Tie the reservation to the specific order/session (e.g. store the reserving order id on the listing, or re-verify order<->listing linkage) and have fulfillPaidSession fail loudly (refund via Stripe + mark the order NEEDS_REVIEW/FAILED) when markSold reports 0 rows updated instead of silently logging; also consider setting an explicit, short Stripe session expiresAt that is <= RESERVATION_TTL so a session can never outlive its reservation.
verifierSummary:
[reachable] isReal=true conf=0.85 sev->HIGH: AFFIRMED as a real defect — I could not find any gate that makes the path unreachable, and every mechanical step in the finding checks out line by line. One genuine mitigating fact lowers severity, but it is itself a blocker slated for fix, so it must not clear this.

Mechanism verified (all paths under /Users/jadyn/Development/IYAE/.claude/worktrees/preprod-audit-report):
1. ResaleService.java:55 `RESERVATION_TTL = Duration.ofMinutes(30)`; `releaseStaleReservations()` (254-264) loads `findByStatusAndReservedAtBefore(RESERVED, now-30m)` and calls `resaleRepo.release(...)` for each. `ResaleListingRepository.release` is `UPDATE ... SET status=LISTED, reservedAt=null WHERE id=:id AND status=RESERVED` — zero reference to orders or payment state. Confirmed: no in-flight-payment check anywhere in the sweep.
2. SchedulerConfig.java:77-84 runs it at `fixedDelay=300000, initialDelay=30000`. The class is a plain `@Configuration @EnableScheduling` with no `@Profile`/condition, so it runs under `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: prod`.
3. CheckoutService.initiateResaleCheckout (247-299) builds `SessionCreateParams` with mode/successUrl/cancelUrl/lineItem/metadata only — I grepped the whole server tree for `setExpiresAt`: zero hits. So the Stripe session keeps its 24h default, 48x the reservation TTL. `release` is called only in the two catch blocks, never on buyer cancel (cancelUrl just returns to /resale/{id}), so the TTL sweep is the only release path.
4. fulfillPaidSession (213-240) guards only on `order.getStatus() == PAID`, then unconditionally sets PAID and calls `resaleService.markSold(order.getResaleListingId())`. markSold (238-244) is `UPDATE ... WHERE status=RESERVED`; 0 rows → `log.info` only. No exception, no refund, no order flag. Confirmed exactly as filed.
5. V16__resale_listings.sql adds `orders.resale_listing_id` as a plain nullable FK with no UNIQUE constraint, so two orders can legitimately point at the same listing — nothing at the DB layer stops the second sale.

Reachability (no refutation available): ResaleController.java:81-84 exposes `POST /api/resale/listings/{id}/checkout`; SecurityConfig only permitAlls `GET /api/resale/listings*` (line 43) and otherwise ends `anyRequest().authenticated()` — so any authenticated buyer reaches it, which the rules say is in scope. web/app/resale/[id]/page.tsx:63 calls `resale.checkout(id)`, so the UI is wired. nginx/conf.d/default.conf proxies /api/ wholesale.

blocking.title: Production pins next@16.2.6, which carries multiple disclosed unauthenticated vulnerabilities including RCE and SSRF in the built-in Image Optimization API
blocking.proof: `npm audit --omit=dev` against the committed package-lock.json shows next@16.2.6 is in the vulnerable range for 17 advisories, including: GHSA-2xp9-vwfh-vxw4 'Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution in Image Optimization API when AVIF files are used' (range >=16.0.0 <16.3.3), GHSA-cjq9-62q9-8jv4 'SSRF in Image Optimization' (range >=16.0.0 <16.3.8), and GHSA-p9j2-gv94-2wf4 'SSRF in rewrites via attacker-controlled destination hostname' (range >=16.0.0 <16.2.11). The app never disables global image optimization (no `images.unoptimized`/`images.remotePatterns` config in next.config.ts; only two `<Image unoptimized>` call sites in app/dashboard/page.tsx cover themselves, not the route), so the built-in `/_next/image` endpoint is live in the standalone server. In production this origin is reachable by any unauthenticated internet client: nginx/conf.d/default.conf's catch-all `location /` proxies anything not matched by `/api/`, `/uploads/`, `/assets/`, or `/_next/static` straight to the `web` upstream, which includes `/_next/image`. `sharp` (next's runtime image-processing dependency, itself flagged HIGH for inherited libvips/libheif/librsvg CVEs) is a genuine runtime dependency of the production Image Optimization code path, not a build-only tool pruned by `output: standalone`. A patched, non-major release (16.4.0) is already available per `npm audit`.
blocking.fix: Bump `next` (and `eslint-config-next`, which is pinned to the same version) to >=16.4.0 in web/package.json and regenerate web/package-lock.json, then rebuild the Docker image before any production deploy. Re-run `npm audit --omit=dev` to confirm the next/postcss/sharp advisories clear.
verifierSummary:
[reachable] isReal=true conf=0.93: Could not refute; every candidate mitigation checked out negative, and the reachability chain is confirmed by direct file reads.

REACHABILITY CONFIRMED:
- nginx/conf.d/default.conf carves out only `location /_next/static` (prefix match). `/_next/image` does not match it and falls through to the catch-all `location / { proxy_pass http://web; }`. docker-compose.prod.yml publishes "80:80"/"443:443" on nginx, so the optimizer is internet-facing to unauthenticated clients.
- web/next.config.ts is the only Next config file and contains NO `images` key (just `output: "standalone"` + rewrites). Image optimization is therefore on by default. The two `unoptimized` props in app/dashboard/page.tsx are per-call-site and do not disable the route. 19 `<Image>` usages across 13 files render local paths through the optimizer, so the endpoint must be functional for the app to render at all.
- web/middleware.ts matcher is "/((?!_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico|api).*)" — it explicitly EXCLUDES _next/image. Middleware neither blocks it nor applies CSP/X-Frame headers to it.
- web/Dockerfile runs `npm ci` from the committed package-lock.json, which pins next 16.2.6 (lock line 8705) with `sharp: "^0.34.5"` as a next optionalDependency (line 8732) — sharp is installed in the deps stage and traced into .next/standalone. The vulnerable version is what ships.
- `npm audit --omit=dev` reproduced locally: next = critical, vulnerable range "9.3.4-canary.0 - 16.3.7", fixAvailable {"next","16.4.0","isSemVerMajor":false}. GHSA-2xp9-vwfh-vxw4 (AVIF RCE, >=16.0.0 <16.3.3) and GHSA-cjq9-62q9-8jv4 (Image Optimization SSRF, >=16.0.0 <16.3.8) both cover 16.2.6, as claimed.
- Attacker influence over optimizer input is stronger than the finding states: `url=` is attacker-supplied, local paths need no remotePatterns, SecurityConfig.java:46 marks /uploads/** permitAll(), and FileStorageService.storeImage validates ONLY the client-supplied Content-Type header (file.getContentType()) with no magic-byte sniffing — so arbitrary bytes (e.g. an AVIF payload) can be stored as .png and sharp will sniff the true format.

MINOR OVER-CLAIMS IN THE FINDING (do not refute it): GHSA-p9j2-gv94-2wf4 (SSRF in rewrites via attacker-controlled destination hostname) is likely inapplicable — this app's rewrite destinations come from the static API_PROXY_TARGET build arg, not request data. Also inapplicable: GHSA-p293-qw3h-jr36 (Windows-only; runtime is node:20-alpine), GHSA-vcvr-r3jv-pc5j (no next/og or ImageResponse usage), and the Server Actions advisories (zero "use server" files). Conversely, additional in-range advisories also apply to this deployment: GHSA-4jqv-mc3x-m676 and GHSA-mcj8-r9mp-w47p (SSG/ISR cache poisoning in self-hosted apps), GHSA-q8wf-6r8g-63ch (image-opt DoS via SVG), GHSA-955p-x3mx-jcvp, and GHSA-6gpp-xcg3-4w24 (Turbopack is Next 16's default builder and there is no i18n config, satisfying "single locale").

SEVERITY: CRITICAL is correct as filed. A critical-rated, internet-reachable RCE surface with a non-semver-major patch (16.4.0) available is a legitimate release blocker; the proposed fix (bump next + eslint-config-next, regenerate the lock, rebuild the image) is accurate and cheap.

[mitigated] isReal=true conf=0.86 sev->HIGH: VERDICT: the finding stands (vulnerable pin, live endpoint, no full mitigation) — but its two load-bearing "unauthenticated" claims are both refuted, so CRITICAL overstates it. Downgrade to HIGH; the fix (bump next to >=16.4.0) is unchanged.

WHAT I CONFIRMED
- Pin is real: /Users/jadyn/Development/IYAE/.claude/worktrees/preprod-audit-report/web/package.json:35 `"next": "16.2.6"`, and package-lock.json resolves node_modules/next to 16.2.6 (eslint-config-next 16.2.6). `npm audit --omit=dev` reproduces the 17 advisories with the ranges quoted in the finding.
- The endpoint is internet-reachable: nginx/conf.d/default.conf has only /api/, /uploads/, /assets/, /_next/static before a catch-all `location / { proxy_pass http://web; }`, so /_next/image reaches the standalone server. web/middleware.ts is not a guard either — its matcher explicitly excludes `_next/image`.
- Image optimization is genuinely live: next.config.ts sets no `images` key at all, and imageConfigDefault (next/dist/shared/lib/image-config.js) has `unoptimized: false`. sharp 0.34.5 plus @img/sharp-linuxmusl-* prebuilds are in package-lock.json and web/Dockerfile runs a plain `npm ci` on node:20-alpine, so the native decoder ships in the runtime image.
- 16.2.6 has no AVIF guard: in next/dist/server/image-optimizer.js, BYPASS_TYPES = [SVG, ICO, ICNS, BMP, JXL, HEIC] — AVIF is absent, detectContentType() sniffs `ftypavif` at offset 4 regardless of the HTTP Content-Type, contentType falls through to JPEG, and optimizeImage() hands the buffer to sharp → libheif. The 16.3.3 "AVIF optimization disabled" mitigation is not present here.

MITIGATIONS I FOUND (partial, not a refutation)
- `remotePatterns: []` / `domains: []` by default: ImageOptimizerCache.validateParams rejects every absolute URL via hasRemoteMatch(). An attacker therefore cannot point /_next/image at their own host; only local paths pass (hasLocalMatch(undefined, …) returns true). This is what demotes the finding.
- Consequence 1: GHSA-cjq9-62q9-8jv4 (SSRF in Image Optimization) is NOT applicable — the advisory states outright "If no `images.remotePatterns` are configured, your app is not affected."
- Consequence 2: GHSA-p9j2-gv94-2wf4 (SSRF in rewrites) is NOT applicable — it requires a destination hostname built from request-controlled input; web/next.config.ts interpolates only `:path*` into the path, with the host coming from the API_PROXY_TARGET env var.
- Also N/A: GHSA-p293-qw3h-jr36 (Windows-hosted only; this is a Linux alpine container) and GHSA-vcvr-r3jv-pc5j (next/og — zero imports of next/og, ImageResponse or opengraph-image in web/app).

WHY IT IS STILL REAL (AVIF RCE path, authenticated)
Local-path fetches go through fetchInternalImage(), which replays the URL through the full Next handler (`handleRequest(mocked.req, …)`), so next.config.ts's `/uploads/:path*` rewrite proxies to the Spring server. The only file-write endpoint in the tree is POST /api/designer/products/upload/image (server/.../controller/DesignerUploadController.java, ROLE_DESIGNER per SecurityConfig and an explicit role check), and FileStorageService.java validates only `file.getContentType()` — the client-supplied multipart header — with no magic-byte check. So AVIF bytes can be stored as `<uuid>.png`, after which `/_next/image?url=/uploads/products/<uuid>.png&w=640&q=75` (640 is in deviceSizes, 75 is the only allowed quality) feeds them to the unpatched AVIF decoder. AuthService blocks only `Role.ADMIN` at registration, so DESIGNER is self-service — but login requires a verified email, so this is an authenticated-with-throwaway-account vector, not "any unauthenticated internet client". I found no unauthenticated way to place attacker-controlled bytes at a Next-fetchable path (no other MultipartFile endpoint; GuestAvatarController takes JSON measurements only).

So: real, no guard closes it, remediation as proposed — but severity HIGH, since every unauthenticated advisory in the cited set is either config-mitigated or platform-N/A, and the critical one needs a self-registered verified designer account. (Residual unauthenticated exposure is limited to the moderate SVG-DoS advisory GHSA-q8wf-6r8g-63ch, reachable via the SVGs shipped in web/public.)

No repo test, config flag, or code path demonstrates the opposite. Severity CRITICAL is correct: npm audit itself grades the next entry critical, and the critical AVIF Image-Optimization RCE sits on a route this deployment leaves enabled and internet-exposed.

blocking.title: rigging-worker silently becomes a second claimant for model/avatar tasks, completing them with mock/stub output
blocking.evidence: task = queue.claim_task()
blocking.proof: main.py's run() polls queue.claim_task() and avatar_queue.claim_task() unconditionally on every iteration, regardless of which container is running or which RIGGING_PROVIDER is configured -- only the rigging claim (line 210) is gated by rigging_enabled. docker-compose.yml's `rigging-worker` service (the documented, supported way to run real Python/Blender garment rigging via `--profile rigging`; worker/Dockerfile.rigging's CMD is also `python main.py`) sets RIGGING_PROVIDER but never sets MODEL_GENERATION_PROVIDER or AVATAR_GENERATION_PROVIDER, so get_provider()/get_avatar_provider() (main.py lines 44-72) default it to StubGenerator and SmplxStubProvider. Once this container is started alongside the primary `worker` service, both processes poll the same model_generation_tasks/avatar_generation_tasks tables with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED; whichever one's SELECT wins a given pending row processes it with ITS configured provider. For every real task the rigging container happens to win, it writes a placeholder empty-scene GLB (or a generic box-mesh avatar) and marks the task READY -- no error, no warning -- which the server then materializes as if it were the designer's real Tripo3D/Meshy model or the user's real SMPL-X avatar.
blocking.fix: Give main.py a way to scope a process to only the queues it should serve (e.g. a WORKER_QUEUES env var gating the queue.claim_task()/avatar_queue.claim_task() calls, not just the rigging one), and set the rigging-worker service to either disable model/avatar polling entirely or mirror the primary worker's real MODEL_GENERATION_PROVIDER/AVATAR_GENERATION_PROVIDER so it never silently substitutes stub output for production tasks.
verifierSummary:
[reachable] isReal=false conf=0.88 sev->LOW: REFUTED for the deployed production configuration. The finding's impact chain requires a second `rigging-worker` container running alongside the primary `worker` with stub model/avatar providers. That container does not exist in production.

Evidence read:

1. `docker-compose.prod.yml` declares exactly six services: `mysql` (2), `server` (19), `worker` (57), `web` (84), `nginx` (105), `certbot` (127). `certbot` is the ONLY profiled service (`profiles: [tools]`, lines 134-135). There is no `rigging-worker` service and no `rigging` profile anywhere in the prod file. `rigging-worker` exists only in `docker-compose.yml:85` (dev), under `profiles: [rigging]`.

2. The single prod `worker` (lines 57-82) is built from `Dockerfile.rigging` and carries all three provider vars coherently: `MODEL_GENERATION_PROVIDER: ${MODEL_GENERATION_PROVIDER:-mock}` (67), `AVATAR_GENERATION_PROVIDER: ${AVATAR_GENERATION_PROVIDER:-mock}` (68), `RIGGING_PROVIDER: ${RIGGING_PROVIDER:-python}` (73). One process, three queues, one provider set — no second claimant and no divergent config. `worker/Dockerfile.rigging:21` is `CMD ["python","main.py"]`, so this one container does serve all three queues (no "rigging tasks never processed" variant either).

3. `prod_deploy.sh:4` pins `COMPOSE_FILE="docker-compose.prod.yml"` and every invocation uses a single `-f "$COMPOSE_FILE"` (lines 114, 125, 127, 150, 157, 164, 172, 177, 206, 210), so `docker-compose.yml` is never merged — `rigging-worker` is not even defined in the production compose project. The only profile prod ever activates is `--profile tools` (150, 164 = certbot), never `--profile rigging`. Its `health` command iterates exactly `mysql server worker web nginx` (line 176).

4. `COMPOSE_PROFILES=rigging` against the prod file would be a no-op — no service there declares that profile. No `docker-compose.override.yml` exists (only the two compose files in the tree), and explicit `-f` suppresses override auto-loading regardless. No k8s/helm manifests. CI (`.github/workflows/e2e.yml:187`) brings up only `mysql server web` — no worker at all.

5. Scaling the prod worker (`--scale worker=N`) cannot trigger this: replicas inherit identical env, so `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` merely distributes work among homogeneous claimants — the documented safe-parallel case.

Where the finding IS live: `dev.sh:34` uses `docker-compose.yml` and `dev.sh:242`/`278` pass `--profile rigging`, so `./dev.sh start` starts BOTH claimants in development, and the dev `rigging-worker` (docker-compose.yml:89-98) omits MODEL_GENERATION_PROVIDER/AVATAR_GENERATION_PROVIDER, defaulting to StubGenerator/SmplxStubProvider. The underlying code weakness is genuine — main.py:138 and :175 poll unconditionally while only the rigging claim at :210 is gated by `rigging_enabled`. But even in dev the primary worker defaults to `mock` too (`.env.example:70`), so output actually diverges only on a dev box configured with a real Meshy/Tripo key. The proposed WORKER_QUEUES scoping is sound defensive hardening and worth doing, but it is not a production data-integrity blocker: severity LOW (dev-ergonomics / latent-robustness), not CRITICAL.

blocking.title: Production nginx has no active TLS: HTTP->HTTPS redirect and the entire HTTPS server block are commented out, and ssl-init does not re-enable them automatically
blocking.evidence: # To enable HTTPS redirect, uncomment the block below.
blocking.proof: The only live server block listens on :80 (line 10) and serves everything over plaintext. The redirect to https (lines 23-25) and the entire `server { listen 443 ssl; ... }` block (lines 72-127, including the HSTS header) are commented out. prod_deploy.sh's `ssl-init` case only runs certbot and restarts nginx; it explicitly does NOT edit the config -- it prints `info "Enable HTTPS block in nginx/conf.d/default.conf and restart nginx"` as a manual follow-up step for the operator. docker-compose.prod.yml maps 443:443 on the nginx container, but nothing inside the container actually listens on 443 until that manual edit happens. As shipped, following the documented path (`./prod_deploy.sh setup` -> `up` -> `ssl-init <domain>`) still leaves the site on HTTP-only unless a human remembers an undocumented-in-the-script manual edit. Every request -- including `POST /api/auth/login` (email+password) and every subsequent request carrying `Authorization: Bearer <jwt>` (HS256, 24h TTL, per server/CLAUDE.md) -- crosses the wire in cleartext. Any network-position attacker (public Wi-Fi, compromised router, ISP-level MITM) who does not need to authenticate to the application at all can passively capture credentials and valid JWTs and fully impersonate any victim for up to 24h.
blocking.fix: Ship the HTTPS server block enabled by default (gated on certificate presence via an nginx variable or a conditional include rather than a commented-out block), have `ssl-init` programmatically uncomment/enable the HTTPS block and the HTTP->HTTPS redirect (and reload nginx) once certbot succeeds, and add HSTS (`Strict-Transport-Security`) to the HTTP response as well so that even a first plaintext visit upgrades future requests once HTTPS is live.

blocking.title: Unauthenticated, enumerable public access to every user's generated body-avatar GLB via /assets/
blocking.evidence: alias /var/iyae/assets/;
blocking.proof: worker/providers/smplx_provider.py (and smplx_stub_provider.py) write each user's generated avatar to `avatars/{user_id}/avatar.glb` and set `glb_url` to `/assets/avatars/{user_id}/avatar.glb`, where `user_id` is the database's sequential auto-increment primary key (confirmed by the comment in server/src/main/java/com/iyae/service/AvatarService.java: "...avatars/{userId}/avatar.glb..., served publicly at /assets/**"). nginx's `location /assets/` (lines 41-45) serves that entire directory tree with a plain filesystem `alias`, no `auth_request`, no token/signature check, and no rate limiting. Avatar GLBs are generated from a user's real body measurements (BodyProfile height/weight/waist/chest/hips via SMPL-X) -- this is biometric-derived PII. An unauthenticated attacker can simply iterate `GET /assets/avatars/1/avatar.glb`, `/2/`, `/3/` ... and mass-download every registered user's personal body-shape model with zero authentication and zero per-request cost beyond nginx's own response time.
blocking.fix: Do not serve per-user generated content (avatars) from a public, unauthenticated static location. Either (a) route avatar GLB reads through an authenticated Spring endpoint that checks ownership/visibility before streaming the file, or (b) if it must stay on nginx static serving, key the path on an unguessable per-asset token/UUID instead of the sequential user id, and consider an `auth_request` subrequest to the API to check viewer permission before nginx serves the file.
verifierSummary:

The only commented-out parts of that file are the HTTPS 301 redirect and the entire `listen 443` block. Grepped all of nginx/nginx.conf and conf.d/default.conf: no `auth_request`, no `satisfy`, no `internal`, no `deny`, no `limit_req` anywhere. No mitigating directive exists.
2. docker-compose.prod.yml — nginx publishes "80:80" to the host and mounts `assets_data:/var/iyae/assets:ro`, so the entire asset tree including `avatars/` is physically present in the container nginx aliases. The worker writes into the same named volume (`WORKER_OUTPUT_DIR: /var/iyae/assets`).
3. Both avatar providers emit the enumerable path, so provider choice does not gate the route: worker/providers/smplx_stub_provider.py:234,248,256 and worker/providers/smplx_provider.py:313,353,362 both write `avatars/{user_id}/avatar.glb` and return `glb_url = /assets/avatars/{user_id}/avatar.glb`.
4. server/src/main/resources/db/migration/V1__*.sql:6 — `users.id BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY`, so `{user_id}` is a sequential integer, trivially iterable.
5. Independent second confirmation that this is unguarded by design, not just by nginx: server/src/main/java/com/iyae/config/SecurityConfig.java:46 — `.requestMatchers("/assets/**", "/uploads/**").permitAll()`, with WebMvcConfig mapping `/assets/**` to `file:/var/iyae/assets/`. Nothing gates the path: no dev-only profile (application-prod.yml only sets logging/show-sql), no feature flag, no dead code, and the URL is live in the UI (web/app/profile/avatar/page.tsx consumes it).

SEVERITY CORRECTION to HIGH — conditional, read before de-prioritising. The access-control hole is 100% real and remotely reachable unauthenticated, but the SENSITIVITY of the leaked bytes depends on one env var that both docker-compose.prod.yml (`AVATAR_GENERATION_PROVIDER: ${AVATAR_GENERATION_PROVIDER:-mock}`) and .env.example:79 (`AVATAR_GENERATION_PROVIDER=mock`) default to `mock`. `mock` resolves to SmplxStubProvider, whose `create_avatar_glb()` emits a HARDCODED 8-vertex / 12-triangle 0.4x1.7x0.25 m box that is byte-identical for every user and explicitly ignores `input_payload` ("Body measurements dict (ignored by stub)"). So on a stock first launch the actual leak is account/user-id enumeration ("user N has generated an avatar"), NOT biometric data — the finding's headline claim of mass-downloading "every registered user's personal body-shape model" is not true of the default deploy. That is the only part I can partially rebut, and it is a severity point, not a reachability one.

BUT `smplx` is a documented, first-class production option, not a dev-only path — prod compose passes the var through AND mounts `${SMPLX_MODELS_PATH}:/var/iyae/smplx_models:ro` into the worker specifically for it. The moment the avatar feature ships for real (it is the product's core 3D try-on value prop; the stub self-describes as "for development and testing"), these GLBs become SMPL-X meshes solved from height/weight/chest/waist/hips and the finding is CRITICAL exactly as filed. Treat HIGH as the floor for a mock-provider launch and restore CRITICAL if `AVATAR_GENERATION_PROVIDER=smplx` is set. Either way it stays blocking: the fix (ownership-checked streaming endpoint, or an unguessable per-asset UUID path) is identical and must land before avatars carry real measurements.

[mitigated] isReal=true conf=0.9 sev->HIGH: Could not refute — I looked for a mitigation on every path and found none. blocking.title: N+1 query pattern across the community feed, followers list, and saved looks (no JOIN FETCH / @EntityGraph)
blocking.proof: PostRepository's feed queries (findByStatusOrderByCreatedAtDesc, findFollowingFeed, findByStatusAndCityOrderByCreatedAtDesc, etc.) return bare Post entities with no JOIN FETCH/@EntityGraph, and Post.user is @ManyToOne(fetch=FetchType.LAZY). For every post in a page, getFeed() calls isLikedBy(p, currentUser) (1 query) then toResponse() -> countByPost (1 query) + countByPost (1 query) + PostResponse.from(post,...) which calls post.getUser().getUsername() (1 lazy-load query). For the default page size of 20, GET /api/posts issues roughly 1 (page fetch) + 20*4 = 81 SQL round-trips inside a single @Transactional(readOnly) method. The identical pattern repeats in FollowService.getFollowers/getFollowing (Follow.follower/following are also LAZY, mapped via f.getFollower()/f.getFollowing() with no fetch join) and in SavedLookService.getSavedLooks (SavedLookRepository.findByUserId has no JOIN FETCH, and extractItemNames() immediately touches the LAZY look.getRecommendation()). This is a real, present-day cost on the most frequently hit endpoint in the app (home/community feed, scrolled repeatedly), and it will scale linearly with feed size and concurrent users, risking DB connection-pool pressure well before the app is otherwise under load. Notably, SavedProductRepository.findByUserIdNewestFirst (a newer, correctly-written sibling) already demonstrates the fix with `JOIN FETCH sp.product p JOIN FETCH p.designerProfile` and a code comment explaining exactly this tradeoff -- confirming the Post/Follow/SavedLook paths are an oversight, not a deliberate design choice.
blocking.fix: Add @EntityGraph(attributePaths={"user"}) (or JOIN FETCH) to the PostRepository feed/user queries, and batch likeCount/commentCount with a single GROUP BY query over the page's post ids instead of one count query per post. Apply the same JOIN FETCH pattern already used in SavedProductRepository.findByUserIdNewestFirst to FollowRepository's follower/following queries and to SavedLookRepository.findByUserId.

blocking.title: Unbounded `size` query parameter on feed/follow/comment pagination allows a single request to bypass pagination entirely
blocking.evidence: Pageable pageable = PageRequest.of(page, size);
blocking.proof: PostController.getFeed/getComments/getByUser and FollowController.getFollowers/getFollowing all accept `@RequestParam(defaultValue = "20") int size` with no upper bound, and the corresponding service methods pass that value straight into `PageRequest.of(page, size)` with no clamp. Any authenticated low-privilege user (BUYER role is enough -- these endpoints only require `anyRequest().authenticated()` per SecurityConfig, not any role check) can call e.g. `GET /api/posts?feed=discover&size=2000000` and force Hibernate to attempt to materialize and JSON-serialize the entire matching result set in one response, defeating pagination and risking heap pressure / long lock/scan time as the posts/follows tables grow. ReviewService already guards exactly this in the same codebase (`private static final int MAX_PAGE_SIZE = 100; ... int clampedSize = Math.min(size, MAX_PAGE_SIZE);`), showing the fix pattern exists but wasn't applied to the newer Post/Follow endpoints.
blocking.fix: Clamp `size` the same way ReviewService does (e.g. `Math.min(size, MAX_PAGE_SIZE)`) inside PostService.getFeed/getComments/getByUser and FollowService.getFollowers/getFollowing, or configure a global `spring.data.web.pageable.max-page-size`.

So the attacker must control a real mailbox, and registration is rate-limited 3/60s per IP. Billed calls are therefore serialized at worker throughput rather than at attacker request rate. This bounds the burst but not cumulative spend, and it converts the flood into indefinite starvation of legitimate designers' generation and avatar tasks — which matches the finding's filed `availability` category.

blocking.title: Guest avatar task creation never supersedes or caps prior tasks for the shared anonymous account
blocking.proof: GuestAvatarController.generate (server/src/main/java/com/iyae/controller/GuestAvatarController.java, lines 18-23) is unauthenticated and backed by a single shared sentinel 'guest' user row (GuestAvatarService.getOrCreateGuestUser, lines 81-93). Unlike the authenticated path, generateForGuest() (lines 39-57) never calls any supersede/cancel logic before inserting a new PENDING AvatarGenerationTask — every call, from every anonymous visitor worldwide, appends another row tied to that one guest account with nothing ever marking earlier abandoned ones FAILED. SchedulerConfig (server/src/main/java/com/iyae/config/SchedulerConfig.java) has no pruning/expiry task for any of the three task tables. The per-IP throttle (RateLimitFilter: 3 requests/60s on POST /api/public/avatar/generate) only bounds a single IP's rate, not the total backlog across all anonymous visitors over time, and the queue is shared with real authenticated users' rows in the same table/worker poll loop. Under organic public traffic (not even an attack — just normal visitors trying the feature and navigating away), the guest user's task backlog grows without bound and with no cleanup, competing with real users' avatar jobs for the same worker capacity.
blocking.fix: Call a supersedeActiveTasks(guest.getId())-style method (mirroring AvatarService.generateAvatar, server/src/main/java/com/iyae/service/AvatarService.java lines 70-71) before inserting a new guest task, and/or add a scheduled cleanup job (SchedulerConfig has no such job today) that expires/fails guest tasks older than a TTL so avatar_generation_tasks can't grow unbounded from anonymous traffic.
verifierSummary:
[reachable] isReal=true conf=0.85 sev->MEDIUM: REACHABLE in production — I could not refute it, so it stands, but the stated impact mechanism is factually wrong and the severity is overstated.

What I verified as TRUE:
1. The route is live and anonymous in prod. `SecurityConfig.filterChain` (server/src/main/java/com/iyae/config/SecurityConfig.java) has `.requestMatchers("/api/public/**").permitAll()`, and `GuestAvatarController` is a plain `@RestController @RequestMapping("/api/public/avatar")` with no `@Profile`/`@ConditionalOnProperty` gate. `nginx/conf.d/default.conf` proxies `location /api/ { proxy_pass http://api; }` with no deny/allow rules, so `POST /api/public/avatar/generate` is internet-reachable in `docker-compose.prod.yml`.
2. `generateForGuest()` really does insert a PENDING row with no supersede. I diffed it against `AvatarService.generateAvatar`, which calls `supersedeActiveTasks(user.getId())` before insert; the guest path has no equivalent call.
3. There is no cleanup/TTL job. `SchedulerConfig` has exactly five `@Scheduled` methods (generation, avatar, rigging, resale-reservation release, weather refresh) — none prunes any task table. `AvatarGenerationTaskRepository` exposes no delete-by-age query.
4. Queue contention is real: `worker/avatar_task_queue.py claim_task()` selects `WHERE status='PENDING' ORDER BY created_at ASC LIMIT 1`, so guest rows sit ahead of authenticated users' rows in one shared FIFO.

What REFUTES the claimed impact (why HIGH is wrong):
- The finding's trigger is "organic public traffic (not even an attack — just normal visitors trying the feature and navigating away)." That feature has no UI. `grep -rn "public/avatar" web/` returns zero hits; `web/lib/api.ts` only exposes the authenticated `avatar` client (`/api/avatar/status|generate|delete`). No page, component, hook, test, or e2e spec calls the guest endpoint. The only non-controller references in the whole repo are `RateLimitFilter`'s rule and three lines of `server/CLAUDE.md`. So organic backlog growth is zero; reaching this requires someone deliberately curling the API.
- `RateLimitFilter` caps it at 3/60s per IP, `app.rate-limit.enabled` defaults true and prod sets `RATE_LIMIT_TRUSTED_PROXIES=172.16.0.0/12` so XFF resolves the real client behind nginx — i.e. the throttle actually works in the prod topology (180 small rows/hour per IP).
- `docker-compose.prod.yml` sets `AVATAR_GENERATION_PROVIDER: ${AVATAR_GENERATION_PROVIDER:-mock}` for both server and worker, so in the default prod config each queued task is a near-instant stub GLB — the "competing with real users' avatar jobs for worker capacity" claim only bites if the operator switches to `smplx`.
- I also checked the secondary amplification the finding implies: stale guest READY rows do not pin forever. `AvatarService.materializeAvatar` skips non-latest READY, but the next 5s cycle promotes the new latest, so the backlog drains one row per cycle rather than accumulating permanently.

Net: a genuine unauthenticated, unbounded-row-growth write surface with no supersede and no TTL (fix as proposed), but behind a working per-IP throttle, with no product path that triggers it and a trivial per-task cost in the default prod provider. That is MEDIUM hygiene/abuse-surface debt, not a HIGH availability risk and not a deployment blocker.

blocking.title: No server-side enforcement against the same owned unit being listed (and sold) more than once
blocking.proof: createListing only checks that the caller purchased productId+size somewhere in their order history (findOwningOrderId) -- it never checks whether an active ResaleListing already exists for that same seller+product+size (that exclusion only happens in the read-only listEligibleItems picker hint, lines 89-92, which the create endpoint never calls). There is also no DB-level uniqueness constraint in V16__resale_listings.sql on (seller_id, product_id, size_label). Two POST /api/resale/listings calls for the same purchased item (a double-submitted form, a client retry after a timeout, two open tabs, or a direct API call) create two independent ResaleListing rows for one physical unit. Each row has its own independent LISTED->RESERVED->SOLD state machine, so Buyer A can reserve+pay listing #1 and Buyer B can reserve+pay listing #2 at the same time -- both are charged via Stripe, but the seller has only one physical item to ship.
blocking.fix: Before creating a listing, check resaleRepo.findBySellerIdAndStatusIn(...) blocking.title: Community feed N+1: per-post like/comment counts and like-status checks on every page of posts
blocking.proof: getFeed/getByUser map every Post in a returned Page through toResponse(), and toResponse() calls postLikeRepository.countByPost(post) + postCommentRepository.countByPost(post); isLikedBy() (called from the same map for a signed-in viewer) adds a third query, postLikeRepository.findByPostAndUser(post, user), per post. A single page of 20 posts on the public community feed therefore issues 1 (feed query) + up to 60 extra round-trips instead of a couple of batched GROUP BY/IN queries. This is the classic N+1 pattern on the app's main social surface (GET /api/posts, hit by every signed-in and anonymous visitor to /community); under normal concurrent traffic this multiplies DB connections/round-trips linearly with page size x request volume, which is a direct resource-exhaustion risk, not a one-off slow query.
blocking.fix: Batch-load like/comment counts and the viewer's liked-post set for the whole page in one or two queries (e.g. SELECT post_id, COUNT(*) FROM post_likes WHERE post_id IN (:ids) GROUP BY post_id, same for comments, and a single findByPostInAndUser for the liked set), then assemble PostResponse from those maps instead of querying per post.

blocking.title: Stripe webhook order lookup has no backing index on orders.stripe_session_id
blocking.evidence: Optional<Order> findByStripeSessionId(String stripeSessionId);
blocking.proof: CheckoutService.fulfillPaidSession (the only path that flips an order PENDING->PAID, clears the cart, and marks resale listings SOLD) calls orderRepository.findByStripeSessionId(session.getId()) inside @Transactional handleWebhook for every Stripe webhook delivery (checkout.session.completed / async_payment_succeeded). orders.stripe_session_id was added in V9__checkout_orders.sql with no UNIQUE constraint and no CREATE INDEX anywhere in V9-V21, and because it's a plain VARCHAR (not a foreign key to another table), it never gets InnoDB's automatic FK-column indexing either -- unlike every FK column in this schema. As the orders table grows, every webhook delivery becomes a full table scan on the orders table; since Stripe retries webhooks with backoff and eventually stops, a slow/scanning lookup here risks orders that are paid in Stripe but never transition to PAID in IYAE under load (stuck PENDING orders, carts that never clear).
blocking.fix: Add a migration: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_orders_stripe_session_id ON orders(stripe_session_id); (unique, since the field is also used as a de-dup key for idempotent webhook handling).

So a user who registers with just email/password/role has username=null in the DB. PostService never backfills or requires a username before allowing posts/comments (grep of PostService.java for "username" returns nothing). blocking.title: DataSeeder's profile guard is a deny-list ("!prod"), so any deployment that doesn't set SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE exactly to "prod" seeds a known-password ADMIN account
blocking.evidence: @Profile("!prod")
blocking.proof: The guard is inverted: it runs on every profile EXCEPT the literal string "prod", rather than only on an explicit allow-list like {"dev","test"}. The two docker-compose files get this right (docker-compose.prod.yml hardcodes SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: prod), but the repo also documents a non-Docker path (root CLAUDE.md "Local Development (without Docker)": `cd server && ./gradlew bootRun`, which defaults to no active profile) that an engineer could point at a shared/staging/production-adjacent MySQL instance (via DB_HOST/DB_USERNAME/DB_PASSWORD env vars) without ever setting the profile. Both the exact seed emails and the exact password are committed in this source file, so no guessing is required: anyone with read access to the repo (or this very file) has working admin credentials for any environment where the profile guard was missed. This is precisely the failure mode the audit brief calls out verbatim ("Seeded demo users with known/weak passwords in production is a CRITICAL"), gated here behind a single easy-to-forget env var rather than a fail-safe allow-list.
blocking.fix: Invert the guard to an explicit allow-list, e.g. `@Profile({"dev","test"})` (or gate on a dedicated `app.seed.enabled` property that defaults to `false` and must be explicitly turned on), so a missing/unrecognized profile fails safe (no seeding) instead of failing open. Independently, stop reusing one weak password across all seeded accounts, especially the ADMIN row — generate a random password per seed run and log/print it once, or require it to come from an env var with no default.

blocking.title: Hardcoded dev fallback for INTERNAL_MAIL_SECRET ships with no runtime safeguard, and the compose file that carries it exposes the web container directly
blocking.evidence: INTERNAL_MAIL_SECRET: ${INTERNAL_MAIL_SECRET:-dev-internal-secret}
blocking.proof: docker-compose.yml's web service publishes the container port directly to the host (`"${WEB_PORT:-3000}:3000"`, line 121) and also carries Traefik labels with a bare Host(`${WEB_DOMAIN}`) rule and no PathPrefix restriction (lines 128-131), plus an `external: true` shared `proxy` network (line 141) — i.e. this compose file is designed to sit behind a real reverse proxy, not just loopback. If this file (rather than docker-compose.prod.yml) is ever brought up on a host reachable from the internet — an easy slip since both files live at the repo root and `docker compose up` defaults to this one — without an operator overriding INTERNAL_MAIL_SECRET in .env, the web container's `process.env.INTERNAL_MAIL_SECRET` is the literal string `dev-internal-secret`, which is published in this same public repo's root CLAUDE.md table. Anyone can then `POST /api/internal/mail/send` with header `x-internal-mail-secret: dev-internal-secret` and an arbitrary `toEmail`/`name`/`actionUrl` to send a branded email from the project's verified Resend sending domain to any recipient, impersonating IYAE for phishing.
blocking.fix: Remove the `:-dev-internal-secret` fallback entirely (match docker-compose.prod.yml's `${INTERNAL_MAIL_SECRET}` with no default) so a missing secret fails closed instead of resolving to a known value, and have route.ts refuse to start/serve (throw at module load, or return 500) if `process.env.INTERNAL_MAIL_SECRET` is empty, rather than only checking it per-request against a request header.

blocking.evidence: require_env_vars DB_PASSWORD MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD JWT_SECRET

blocking.title: Production container runs as root with no non-root USER, directly amplifying the next.js RCE above
blocking.evidence:
FROM node:20-alpine AS runner
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production
ENV HOSTNAME=0.0.0.0
COPY --from=builder /app/.next/standalone ./
COPY --from=builder /app/.next/static ./.next/static
COPY --from=builder /app/public ./public
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
blocking.proof: The runner stage has no `USER` instruction anywhere, so `node server.js` runs as root (uid 0) inside the container. Combined with the previous finding: if an attacker exploits the disclosed next@16.2.6 Image Optimization RCE (GHSA-2xp9-vwfh-vxw4) to get code execution in this container, that code executes as root rather than being confined to an unprivileged account -- unrestricted filesystem access inside the container and a stronger foothold for any container-escape or lateral-movement attempt against the other services on the shared `iyae-net` bridge network (mysql, server, worker). The base image, `node:20-alpine`, is also a floating tag (not pinned to a digest) on a Node.js release line whose LTS maintenance window has already closed as of today's date, so the OS/runtime layer itself is no longer receiving security backports without an explicit, deliberate version bump.
blocking.fix: Add a dedicated non-root user/group in the runner stage (e.g. `RUN addgroup -g 1001 nodejs && adduser -u 1001 -G nodejs -S nextjs`), `chown` the copied `.next/standalone`, `.next/static`, and `public` directories to it, and add `USER nextjs` before `CMD`. Separately, move off `node:20-alpine` to a currently-maintained LTS line (22 or 24) and pin to a digest (`node:22-alpine@sha256:...`) rather than a floating major tag.

3. grep for `user:`, `security_opt`, `read_only`, `cap_drop`, `no-new-privileges` across both compose files returns NOTHING. No compose-level `user:` override reinstates an unprivileged uid; no capabilities dropped; no no-new-privileges. The process retains Docker's default root capability set.
4. nginx/conf.d/default.conf:47-54 — `location /_next/static` and `location /` both proxy_pass to http://web, and nginx publishes 80:80/443:443 (compose lines 107-109). The root-running Next.js server is on the unauthenticated public request path.

blocking.title: fail_task() has no RUNNING guard -- can overwrite an already-completed (READY) task back to FAILED
blocking.evidence: WHERE id = %s
blocking.proof: complete_task() (same file, line 63) and rigging_task_queue.fail_task() (line 83: `WHERE id = %s AND status = 'RUNNING'`) both guard their UPDATE on the task still being RUNNING, explicitly to prevent a superseded attempt from resurrecting/clobbering a later one. task_queue.fail_task() and avatar_task_queue.fail_task() (same file, line 80) have no such guard -- just `WHERE id = %s`. If a task is reclaimed and re-claimed by a second worker (see the CRITICAL finding and the stale-reclaim race below) while the original attempt's provider.generate() call is still in flight, and the second attempt successfully completes the task to READY, the original attempt's eventual exception/timeout will call queue.fail_task(task_id, str(e)) -- which unconditionally flips the row from READY to FAILED, even though a valid output_payload and GLB file exist. A designer/buyer-facing status now falsely reports failure for a generation that actually succeeded.
blocking.fix: Add `AND status = 'RUNNING'` to the WHERE clause in task_queue.fail_task() and avatar_task_queue.fail_task(), mirroring rigging_task_queue.fail_task() and the existing complete_task() guards.
verifierSummary:
[reachable] isReal=true conf=0.85 sev->LOW: The code defect is real and the guard asymmetry is exactly as described: task_queue.py:77-81 and avatar_task_queue.py:77-81 use bare `WHERE id = %s`, while complete_task in both files (line 63) and rigging_task_queue.fail_task both carry `AND status = 'RUNNING'` with a comment stating the guard exists to stop superseded attempts from clobbering later ones. So the finding is not a fabrication and I do not refute it.

But the HIGH severity rests on a precondition the deployed production configuration does not satisfy, and I verified that affirmatively:

(1) prod_deploy.sh:4 pins COMPOSE_FILE="docker-compose.prod.yml" for every subcommand; that file declares exactly ONE `worker` service (lines 57-82) with no deploy.replicas, the script never passes --scale, and there are no k8s/helm/other orchestrator manifests in the tree. worker/Dockerfile.rigging ends in a single `CMD ["python", "main.py"]` — one process.

(2) worker/main.py is a single-threaded `while True` loop with no threading. reclaim_stale_tasks() for all three queues runs at the TOP of that same loop (`if poll_count % 12 == 0`, lines 113-132), so it cannot run while the process is blocked inside provider.generate() (lines 146/183). A lone worker therefore can never reclaim its own in-flight task, and can never have two attempts on one task_id concurrently.

(3) The only other writer to these rows, the Spring server, never sets READY: GenerationService.supersedeActiveTasks does PENDING/RUNNING -> FAILED (lines 102-103), retry() does FAILED -> PENDING (line 128), materialize does READY -> MATERIALIZED (line 182). READY is thus written exclusively by the single worker process holding the claim, and per claim it calls complete_task XOR fail_task.

Consequently the claimed impact — a row with a valid output_payload and an on-disk GLB silently flipped READY -> FAILED, showing a user a false failure for a generation that succeeded — requires two concurrent processors of the same task id and is NOT reachable at one replica. The second main.py poller (rigging-worker) exists only in the dev docker-compose.yml behind `profiles: [rigging]`.

I still return isReal=true rather than refuting, for two reasons. First, a narrower harm IS reachable single-worker: between claim and fail the server can move the row to PENDING (regenerate supersedes the in-flight row to FAILED, making it the latest FAILED row, then the designer retry endpoint sets it PENDING), and the unguarded fail_task then stomps PENDING -> FAILED, silently discarding a re-queue that complete_task's guard was written to honor; it also overwrites the "Superseded by regeneration" error_message. Non-destructive and self-healing (retry again), but real. Second, the single-replica invariant is operational, not structural: the worker is a stateless container, worker/CLAUDE.md:420 itself asserts "SKIP LOCKED ensures multiple worker instances can run safely in parallel", and `docker compose up -d --scale worker=2` reinstates the full race with zero code change — I will not certify a release on a config property one flag breaks.

Severity should be LOW, not HIGH: the data-integrity corruption that would justify HIGH is gated on concurrency absent from prod, leaving a latent hazard plus a narrow self-healing re-queue clobber; the fix is a two-word SQL addition. Raise to MEDIUM if the launch plan involves running more than one worker container, or if the sibling CRITICAL finding this one cites establishes same-task-id concurrency by a mechanism I did not see in the committed config.

[mitigated] isReal=true conf=0.92 sev->MEDIUM: NOT REFUTED. The code facts are exactly as filed, and I found no mitigation at any layer.

Verified code:

- `worker/rigging_task_queue.py:80-84` — `WHERE id = %s AND status = 'RUNNING'`. The guard exists on the third queue, so this is an omission, not a design with a compensating control.
- `complete_task` in both unguarded files (`task_queue.py:63`, `avatar_task_queue.py:63`) carries the guard with the comment "prevents superseded (FAILED) tasks from resurrecting" — it protects only the opposite direction.

Mitigations I looked for and did NOT find:
- DB layer: `V1__baseline_schema.sql:78` declares `status ENUM('PENDING','RUNNING','READY','FAILED')`. `grep -rn "TRIGGER|CHECK ("` over all 21 migrations returns nothing. Nothing rejects a READY→FAILED or MATERIALIZED→FAILED transition.
- JPA optimistic locking: no `@Version` on `ModelGenerationTask`/`AvatarGenerationTask`.
- Server-side compensation: `GenerationService.getStatus` (line 57) gates `glbUrl`/`usdzUrl` strictly on `status == READY || MATERIALIZED`, so a clobbered row surfaces as FAILED with the error message. `processReadyTasks` (line 145) selects `findByStatus(READY)`, so a row clobbered inside the 5s scheduler window is never materialized — the generated GLB on disk is orphaned and no `GarmentAsset` row is ever created. The claimed impact is accurate.

Why MEDIUM, not HIGH — the filed trigger is materially less reachable than stated in the shipped topology:
1. `docker-compose.prod.yml` defines exactly ONE `worker` service (no `replicas`/`deploy.replicas`; `prod_deploy.sh` has no scale flag). `worker/main.py`'s loop is single-threaded and strictly sequential: while an attempt is blocked inside `provider.generate()` (line 146), that same thread cannot run `reclaim_stale_tasks()` (line 115), and `claim_task` only selects `status='PENDING'`. One process cannot produce the two concurrent attempts the finding's scenario needs.
2. Reclaim fires at `updated_at < NOW() - INTERVAL 15 MINUTE`, but both model providers cap polling at `range(120)` × 5s = 10 min with `timeout=30/10/60` on every HTTP call, so a typical worst-case attempt is ~12-13 min — under the threshold. (Not impossible: `timeout=60` on the streamed download is per-read, not a total-transfer cap.)

But it is genuinely reachable, so it cannot be cleared:
- Dev `--profile rigging` starts a SECOND `python main.py` (`worker/Dockerfile.rigging:21` has the same CMD), and that process polls and reclaims ALL THREE queues including model+avatar — the full race is live there. `worker/CLAUDE.md` also advertises "SKIP LOCKED ensures multiple worker instances can run safely in parallel" as a design property, which this asymmetry silently breaks for anyone who scales out.
- Single-worker path the finding misses: with no status guard at all, `fail_task` also clobbers PENDING. `GenerationService.retry` (line 128) sets the SAME row FAILED→PENDING. Sequence on one worker: task claimed → RUNNING, generate in flight; designer regenerates (`supersedeActiveTasks`, line 103, sets it FAILED); designer retries (row → PENDING); the still-in-flight old attempt throws → `fail_task` flips PENDING→FAILED and no worker ever runs that queued retry.

The proposed one-line fix (`AND status = 'RUNNING'`) closes all of these and matches the existing pattern.

blocking.title: Stale-task reclamation has no heartbeat and no attempt cap, enabling duplicate processing and unbounded poison-task retries
blocking.evidence: AND updated_at < NOW() - INTERVAL 15 MINUTE
blocking.proof: model_generation_tasks.updated_at has ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP (V1__baseline_schema.sql) and is only touched once, by claim_task()'s UPDATE; nothing refreshes it while provider.generate() is running, so the 15-minute staleness clock is frozen at claim time for the entire processing duration. blocking.title: Rigging pipeline silently rebinds numerically-degenerate vertices to the pelvis with no error, log, or validation catch
blocking.evidence: w = np.where(w >= top_k_threshold, w, 0.0)
blocking.proof: Chain (verified by reading the code plus an actual numpy reproduction of the exact sequence of operations): (1) mesh_preflight.py's _find_loose_vertices() is explicitly WARN-only ('if loose > 0: logger.warning(...)', never added to the `errors` list returned by preflight_mesh), so a garment GLB with a loose/unreferenced vertex (a common artifact of generative/retopologized meshes) passes preflight. (2) In weight_transfer.find_closest_surface_matches, a loose vertex has no adjacent faces, so trimesh's vertex_normals for it is the zero vector; the angle guard `if gn_len > 1e-8: ...` leaves gn as [0,0,0], making `dot = clip(dot([0,0,0], interp_n), -1, 1) == 0`, which is always < cos(75 deg) (~0.259), so the vertex is always classified unmatched regardless of distance. (3) In inpaint_weights, that vertex's row in the global sparse Laplacian is degenerate (no edges), which is the textbook condition for scipy.sparse.linalg.spsolve to return NaN/Inf for the corresponding unknowns without raising a Python exception (a documented SciPy/SuperLU behavior for singular systems) -- and even the `except Exception -> lsqr` fallback path is not guaranteed NaN-free for a rank-deficient block. I did not execute robust_laplacian itself (heavy dep, not installed in this environment) to 100% nail the exact numeric output, but no code anywhere in weight_transfer.py, python_rigging_provider.py, or skinned_glb_writer.py calls np.isnan/np.nan_to_num on the solved weights (confirmed via grep) -- there is no guard between the solve and `np.clip(x_free, 0.0, 1.0)` in inpaint_weights, and np.clip propagates NaN unchanged. (4) I verified empirically (python3 + numpy) that if even ONE value in a vertex's 55-length weight row is NaN, `top_k_threshold = np.partition(w,-4,axis=1)[:, -4:].min(...)` becomes NaN (NaN sorts as the maximum in numpy partition/sort), and the line at weight_transfer.py:204 `np.where(w >= NaN, w, 0.0)` then evaluates its condition False for every column (NaN comparisons are always False) -- wiping the ENTIRE row, including any legitimate non-NaN weights in that row, to zero. (5) That now-all-zero row then hits the `zero_rows` fallback in dense_weights_to_top4 (weight_transfer.py:249-253), which silently rebinds the vertex 100% to joint index 0 (pelvis) with no warning or log line anywhere. (6) validate_skin_metadata (worker/validator.py:298-347) and validate_rigged_glb only check that JOINTS_0/WEIGHTS_0 attributes are PRESENT and shape-consistent -- they never decode the buffer bytes to check the actual weight values, so this defect passes validation and the task is marked READY/MATERIALIZED. End result: a garment with even one preflight-tolerated loose vertex near a seam/hem can ship a rigged GLB where that vertex is glued to the pelvis instead of following its intended body part during pose animation -- a visibly broken try-on render for a product explicitly central to the app's pitch (3D/AR virtual try-on) -- with zero signal anywhere (no failed task, no warning log, no validation error) pointing at the cause.
blocking.fix: Add an explicit NaN/Inf guard immediately after the spsolve/lsqr call in inpaint_weights (e.g. `x_free = np.nan_to_num(x_free, nan=0.0, posinf=1.0, neginf=0.0)` before the existing np.clip), and log + count how many vertices needed this fallback so the PENETRATION_AUDIT-style audit line in main.py can surface a 'RIGGING_AUDIT: N vertices defaulted to pelvis' metric. Longer term, extend validate_skin_metadata (or add a sibling check) to decode the WEIGHTS_0/JOINTS_0 buffers and fail the task if any weight is NaN/Inf or if an implausible fraction of vertices are bound solely to joint 0, so a degenerate rig fails closed instead of shipping silently.
