advisory.title: useGenerationStatus has no AbortController -- the race class fixed in sibling hooks was not applied here
advisory.proof: web/CLAUDE.md's own changelog documents that useRiggingStatus and useOutfitRiggingStatus were hardened against exactly this class of bug (a stale response from a superseded request overwriting newer state) because Next.js App Router does not unmount the page when a dynamic segment's param changes (PDP -> PDP, or here designer/products/[id]/edit -> designer/products/[id]/edit). useGenerationStatus (consumed by web/components/GenerationStatusCard.tsx, rendered on web/app/designer/products/[id]/edit/page.tsx) still has none of that protection: it has no AbortController at all, so if a designer navigates from editing product A to product B without a full reload, a slow in-flight response for A can resolve after B's request and overwrite B's status with A's PENDING/RUNNING/FAILED/retryCount data -- and the 5s poll interval can similarly let two overlapping ticks land out of order. The resulting bad state self-corrects on the next 5s poll (bounding the impact), which is why this is MEDIUM rather than HIGH, but it is a visible wrong-status flash on a designer-facing page that the same CLAUDE.md changelog says this exact pattern was supposed to have been swept for ('look for the same class elsewhere').
advisory.fix: Thread an AbortSignal through loadStatus/fetchStatus (mirroring web/lib/hooks/useRiggingStatus.ts, which takes loadStatus(signal: AbortSignal), gates every commit on !signal.aborted, and aborts the previous in-flight request before starting a new one), and add a useEffect(() => () => controller.abort(), [])-style cleanup so neither the mount fetch nor the 5s poll can commit state after the hook's inputs have moved on.

advisory.title: FittingHelper mutates materials shared by drei's GLTF cache, not per-instance clones
advisory.proof: Three.js's Object3D.clone() (used in AvatarViewer.tsx:107 scene.clone() for GarmentModel) and SkeletonUtils.clone() (used in AvatarViewer.tsx:168/126 cloneSkeleton(scene) for BoundGarmentModel/AvatarModel) are documented/well-known to be shallow with respect to materials and geometry: a Mesh.copy() assigns this.material = source.material (same reference, only the array wrapper is sliced) rather than deep-cloning it. Combined with drei's useGLTF returning the exact same cached scene object for every component that loads the same URL (confirmed via web/node_modules/suspend-react/index.cjs.js's cache being keyed by [loader, url]), every clone of a given GLB across the app shares the same underlying MeshStandardMaterial instances. applyGarmentNormalMap's guard (!mat.normalMap) means only the first mount of a given GLB in a session picks its slot-keyed normal map (web/lib/fabric-textures.ts config varies by slot) -- a later mount of the same GLB under a different slot (e.g. the no-slot path at AvatarViewer.tsx:303-305, <GarmentModel key={...} url={url} /> with no slot prop, reused as a static fallback for an item that was rigged with a slot elsewhere in the session) silently keeps whatever normal map/anti-penetration offset the first mount set, rather than the value its own slot would produce. I could not trace a concrete occurrence of the exact same product GLB being rendered under two different slots in this codebase's current data, so I can't confirm this fires in practice today -- flagging as MEDIUM latent-correctness risk rather than a confirmed user-visible bug.
advisory.fix: If a garment GLB can legitimately be rendered under more than one slot context in the same session, clone the material (or geometry, for anti-penetration polygonOffset tuning) before mutating it in fabricizeMaterial/applyGarmentNormalMap/applyLayeredAntiPenetration, e.g. mesh.material = mat.clone() before setting properties -- otherwise document that every GLB's slot assignment is expected to be fixed for the life of the session and this is intentionally cheap, idempotent mutation.

advisory.title: Resale listing detail page gets stuck on the loading skeleton forever for a malformed/zero id
advisory.proof: `id = Number(params.id)` (line 33). For any URL segment that is not a positive integer string (e.g. `/resale/abc` → NaN, or `/resale/0` → 0, or an empty path segment → 0), `!id` is true and the effect returns before the `.finally(() => setLoading(false))` ever runs. `loading` was initialised to `true` and nothing else ever flips it, so the page renders the `Skeleton` loading state indefinitely with no error message and no way to recover short of navigating away — a dead end for any user who follows a stale bookmark, a malformed share link, or mistypes a listing id.
advisory.fix: Validate `id` up front (e.g. `const id = Number(params.id); const idValid = Number.isInteger(id) && id > 0;`) and short-circuit straight to the existing error UI (`setError('Listing not found.')`) instead of silently skipping the effect, mirroring the pattern already used for a failed fetch on this same page.

advisory.title: Switching AI chat sessions while a reply is in flight appends the stale session's response into the newly selected session
advisory.evidence:
const response = await chat.sendMessage(sessionId, text);
        setMessages((prev) => [...prev, response]);
advisory.proof: `handleSelectSession` (line 260-263) is not gated on `isSending` and simply calls `setActiveSessionId(id)`, which the sidebar lets the user click at any time — including while an AI reply for the previous session is still pending (a real LLM call can take several seconds). `sendMessageToSession` closes over a `sessionId` it resolves once at call time, but the `await chat.sendMessage(...)` response is appended via `setMessages(prev => [...prev, response])` with no check that `activeSessionId` is still the session that originated the request. Meanwhile the 'load messages when session changes' effect (lines 211-238) has already replaced `messages` with the newly selected session's history. The result: session A's reply (and A's optimistic user bubble, line 282) visibly lands in session B's transcript on screen, even though the server correctly stored it under session A — confusing cross-session contamination that only resolves itself on the next full reload/refetch of session B.
advisory.fix: Guard the response commit on the session that originated it, e.g. keep a ref of the session id the request was sent for and skip `setMessages`/`setCurrentSuggestions` if `activeSessionId` (read from a ref, not the stale closure) has since changed — the same pattern already used elsewhere in this codebase (`useRiggingStatus`, `products/page.tsx`) to gate a commit on signal/identity rather than letting a resolved promise write unconditionally.

advisory.title: Email template interpolates actionUrl into an href attribute without HTML-escaping
advisory.fix: HTML-attribute-escape actionUrl (at minimum escape `"` and `<`/`>`) before interpolating it, matching the escapeHtml() treatment already applied to title/bodyText/actionText/footnote, and have the route validate that actionUrl's origin matches the configured FRONTEND_BASE_URL before rendering.

advisory.title: No rate limiting or payload-size cap on the internal mail route itself
advisory.fix: Add a request-rate cap (reusing the pattern already used server-side, e.g. a small fixed-window limiter) and an explicit body-size guard in the route itself, so the route doesn't rely solely on the Java server's own RateLimitFilter for protection if this endpoint is ever reached by another path.

advisory.title: next.config.ts's /api, /uploads, /assets rewrites are not actually dev-only -- they ship unconditionally in the production image with no validation of the baked-in API_PROXY_TARGET
advisory.proof: next.config.ts has no environment branching (no NODE_ENV check), so this rewrite -- and the matching /uploads and /assets rewrites -- compile into the production standalone server exactly as they do in dev, pointed at whatever API_PROXY_TARGET build ARG was supplied (web/Dockerfile line 10: `ARG API_PROXY_TARGET=http://server:8080`). docker-compose.prod.yml currently supplies the correct value (http://server:8080), and nginx's dedicated `location /api/` block normally intercepts /api/* before it ever reaches the web container in production, so this is not an active bug today. But there is no build-time or startup check that the baked value resolves to anything real, and any container on the shared iyae-net bridge network (including, after the two findings above, a compromised web container itself) can reach web:3000/api/* directly, bypassing nginx and whatever edge protections it adds. A future change to the nginx config, a build run outside docker-compose.prod.yml, or a typo in the compose override would silently ship a wrong/unreachable backend target with no signal until live API traffic fails.
advisory.fix: Either gate the proxy rewrite on process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production' so it genuinely cannot be reached outside dev, or add a startup assertion (e.g. in a custom server bootstrap or a healthcheck) that fails fast if API_PROXY_TARGET is unset/unreachable, rather than relying on nginx alone to make the Next.js-side rewrite moot.

advisory.title: Visible focus indicator removed from the Sort control on the product catalog page
advisory.evidence: className="h-auto gap-1 border-0 bg-transparent p-0 text-[12px] font-medium uppercase tracking-[0.12px] text-foreground shadow-none focus:ring-0"
advisory.fix: Drop `focus:ring-0` (or replace it with an explicit `focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-ring focus-visible:ring-offset-2` so the trigger keeps its minimal chrome but still gets a visible indicator on keyboard focus).

advisory.title: Community post detail modal has no accessible name, plus a redundant unlabeled icon-only close button
advisory.fix: Wrap the existing 'Comments' heading text (line ~286-288) in `<DialogTitle>` (visually-hidden via `sr-only` if the current look must be kept) so the dialog has an accessible name. Add `aria-label="Close"` to the custom close button at lines 296-301, or remove it and rely on the DialogContent primitive's own correctly-labeled close control.

advisory.title: Skip-to-content link has no matching landmark on most primary pages — `#main-content` only exists via PageShell
advisory.fix: Add `id="main-content"` to the `<main>` element on every page that doesn't use `<PageShell>` (products/page.tsx both the loaded and Suspense-fallback `<main>`, register/page.tsx's `<main>`, community/page.tsx's `<main>`), and add a `<main id="main-content">` wrapper to pages that currently render no `<main>` landmark at all (login/page.tsx, try-on/page.tsx, and the homepage via components/home/immersive-homepage.tsx). Simplest long-term fix: standardize every page shell on `<PageShell>` (web/components/PageShell.tsx:10), which already sets the id.

advisory.title: No SIGTERM handling -- container stop/redeploy kills an in-flight task ungracefully
advisory.proof: The only graceful-shutdown path in run() is `except KeyboardInterrupt`, which Python raises only for SIGINT. `docker stop` / `docker compose restart` / a rolling redeploy (prod_deploy.sh update) send SIGTERM, which Python's default handler terminates the process on immediately -- no exception is raised, so this except block is never reached. A task that is mid-flight inside provider.generate() when that happens is left at status=RUNNING with no commit ever happening for it, and recovery depends entirely on the stale-reclaim mechanism shown above to be racy and (for model/avatar queues) uncapped on attempts.
advisory.fix: Register a SIGTERM handler (`signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, ...)`) that sets a flag checked at the top of the loop, allowing the current task to finish (or be abandoned cleanly with an explicit fail/requeue) before exiting, rather than relying on an abrupt kill.

advisory.title: No retry/backoff on transient 429/5xx from Meshy/Tripo — a single rate-limit or transient server error fails the whole multi-minute generation attempt
advisory.fix: Use a requests.Session with a urllib3 Retry (status_forcelist=[429,500,502,503,504], backoff_factor, respecting Retry-After) for the task-create and poll requests in both MeshyGenerator and TripoGenerator, so a transient provider-side error during the up-to-10-minute poll loop doesn't immediately fail the task.

advisory.title: PythonRiggingProvider has no execution timeout or mesh-size cap, unlike BlenderRiggingProvider, and runs synchronously inside the single-threaded worker poll loop
advisory.proof: worker/main.py polls model_generation_tasks, avatar_generation_tasks, and rigging_tasks in one synchronous loop (also doing the 12-cycle stale-task reclaim) with no per-call timeout wrapper around `rigging_provider.generate(...)`. BlenderRiggingProvider explicitly bounds its work via `subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=_BLENDER_TIMEOUT)` (blender_rigging_provider.py:126-131, _BLENDER_TIMEOUT=300s), but PythonRiggingProvider.generate() runs entirely in-process: a per-vertex Python loop in weight_transfer.find_closest_surface_matches, a scipy sparse biharmonic solve in inpaint_weights, and a second global igl BVH query in penetration_pushout -- none of which has any wall-clock or size limit of its own. mesh_preflight.preflight_mesh (worker/providers/mesh_preflight.py) only rejects on non-manifold-edge/degenerate-face counts, never on raw vertex/triangle count. The only indirect bound is the unrelated model-generation validator's MAX_TRIANGLE_COUNT=500000 cap (validator.py), which the source garment GLB happens to have already passed before rigging -- far above what Meshy normally requests (target_polycount=30000 per worker/CLAUDE.md), so a garment that is unusually dense (still under 500k) or that hits a slow/degenerate sparse-solve case would stall the worker process for the whole duration with no recovery path other than an external kill/restart -- during which ALL pending model, avatar, and rigging tasks for every product are blocked, since this is the only worker process polling all three queues.
advisory.fix: Run PythonRiggingProvider.generate() under an explicit deadline (e.g. execute it in a worker subprocess/thread pool with a timeout analogous to BLENDER_TIMEOUT, or wrap with a signal-based alarm on platforms that support it), and add an explicit vertex/triangle ceiling check in mesh_preflight before the expensive Phase 1-3 calls so an oversized mesh fails fast with a clear error instead of degrading worker availability.

advisory.title: BlenderRiggingProvider's avatar_glb_url is never populated by the server -- RIGGING_PROVIDER=blender would fail every rigging task
advisory.proof: server/src/main/java/com/iyae/service/RiggingService.java (requestRigging, lines 58-61 and retry's backfill path, lines 141-144) only serializes `source_glb_url` and `slot_hint` into the task's input_payload JSON -- `avatar_glb_url` is never included, even though RiggingTask.java has a dedicated `avatarGlbUrl` column that is likewise never populated anywhere in RiggingService. Because of this, `input_payload.get("avatar_glb_url", "")` in BlenderRiggingProvider.generate() always resolves to an empty string, `_resolve_path("")` returns it unchanged, and the job.json written to disk carries `avatar_glb_url: ""`. worker/providers/blender_scripts/rig_garment.py's `_import_avatar_with_armature(bpy, job["avatar_glb_url"])` then calls `bpy.ops.import_scene.gltf(filepath="")`, which raises inside Blender's own try/except and is reported back as `failure_code: BLENDER_EXPORT_FAILED` for every single task. This means the `RIGGING_PROVIDER=blender` option documented in the env var table (worker/CLAUDE.md) is 100% non-functional in the current server integration regardless of whether Blender is installed and configured correctly -- an operator who follows the documented instructions to switch to it would see every rigging task fail with no indication that the root cause is a missing server-side field, not a Blender/environment problem.
advisory.fix: Either wire a real avatar GLB path (e.g. a pre-generated canonical SMPL-X A-pose avatar asset) into RiggingService.requestRigging's input_payload before any environment is allowed to set RIGGING_PROVIDER=blender, or explicitly mark/gate the Blender provider as unsupported (remove it from the documented option list, or have get_rigging_provider() in main.py refuse to start with RIGGING_PROVIDER=blender) until that wiring exists.

advisory.title: Stale 'git lfs pull' remediation advice baked into runtime error/log messages
advisory.evidence: "(%d bytes). Run 'git lfs pull' to download actual model files.",
advisory.proof: The repo has no .gitattributes and no LFS tracking anywhere (confirmed: `cat .gitattributes` is empty/absent; `git check-ignore -v` shows the model files are excluded via a plain `.gitignore` rule, not LFS). smplx_models/README.md explicitly says the models 'previously lived in Git LFS' (past tense) and documents `scripts/fetch-smplx-models.sh` as the current install mechanism. If AVATAR_GENERATION_PROVIDER=smplx is enabled in production and the weights are missing/corrupted, every avatar task fails with a RuntimeError telling the on-call engineer to run `git lfs pull` -- a no-op against a gitignored, non-LFS path (and git-lfs may not even be installed on the host) -- sending them down a dead end during an incident instead of the one command (`fetch-smplx-models.sh`) that actually fixes it.
advisory.fix: Update the three Git-LFS-specific messages (around lines 93, 123, 187-188) and the `_is_lfs_pointer`/`_resolve_smplx_model_path` docstrings to point at `./scripts/fetch-smplx-models.sh --check` / `./scripts/fetch-smplx-models.sh <archive>`, which is the actual (non-LFS) mechanism documented in smplx_models/README.md.

advisory.title: Dockerfile.rigging omits the CPU-only torch index used by the base Dockerfile — production worker image pulls the CUDA-bundled wheel
advisory.proof: worker/Dockerfile (line 7) explicitly does `pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu` before installing the rest of requirements.txt, so that `torch>=2.0.0` in requirements.txt is already satisfied with the small CPU-only wheel. Dockerfile.rigging skips that step and goes straight to `pip install -r requirements.txt` (line 11), so pip resolves `torch` against the default PyPI index, which for Linux pulls the GPU/CUDA-enabled build together with its `nvidia-cuda-*`/`nvidia-cublas-*` transitive dependencies (multiple GB) — on a host with no GPU. docker-compose.prod.yml's single `worker` service builds from exactly this Dockerfile (`dockerfile: Dockerfile.rigging`, line 60), so this is the image actually shipped to production, not just an optional dev profile.
advisory.fix: In Dockerfile.rigging, install torch from the CPU wheel index the same way the base Dockerfile does, before `pip install -r requirements.txt`: `RUN pip install --no-cache-dir torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu`.

advisory.title: All runtime dependencies are unpinned (floor-only `>=`), including compatibility-sensitive ML packages — no lock file or upper bound
advisory.proof: Every dependency in requirements.txt (mysql-connector-python, requests, torch, smplx, trimesh, Pillow, numpy, scipy, pygltflib) is a floor-only `>=` range with no upper bound, pin, or lock file (no requirements.lock / pip-compile output / hashes, and no pyproject.toml exists in worker/). `./prod_deploy.sh update` runs `docker compose build` from scratch each time, so an unrelated code change (or just a rebuild on a day a new major release of numpy/torch/trimesh lands) can silently pull an incompatible version — e.g. a numpy 2.x bump breaking smplx/trimesh/pygltflib's C-extension ABI — and break avatar/rigging generation in production with no corresponding code diff and no CI guard to catch the drift ahead of the deploy.
advisory.fix: Pin exact versions (or add a compiled lock file via pip-compile/uv) for the heavy/compatibility-sensitive packages at minimum (torch, numpy, smplx, trimesh, scipy, pygltflib), and add a CI job that rebuilds the worker image periodically against unpinned ranges to catch drift before it reaches a deploy.

advisory.title: Model/avatar/rigging provider selection silently falls back to the mock/stub provider on a missing or misspelled env var, with no deploy-time guard
advisory.proof: `.env.example` ships `MODEL_GENERATION_PROVIDER=mock` / `AVATAR_GENERATION_PROVIDER=mock` / `RIGGING_PROVIDER=mock` as the literal values meant for local dev (lines 70, 79, 91), and `prod_deploy.sh setup` copies `.env.example` to `.env` verbatim when `.env` doesn't exist (lines 90-92). `require_env_vars` (prod_deploy.sh line 107) only validates `DB_PASSWORD MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD JWT_SECRET` — it never checks that the generation provider vars were overridden for production. If an operator deploys without changing them (or typos the var name), `get_provider()`/`get_avatar_provider()`/`get_rigging_provider()` in main.py all fall through to their `else` branch and silently return the Stub provider. The worker still completes every task as READY (StubGenerator's placeholder GLBs pass all validators), so real designers' products get served empty box-mesh 3D previews in production with only an INFO-level startup log line (`Model provider: StubGenerator`) as the sole signal — no WARN/ERROR, and docker-compose.prod.yml itself encodes the same silent default (`MODEL_GENERATION_PROVIDER: ${MODEL_GENERATION_PROVIDER:-mock}`, line 67).
advisory.fix: Have `prod_deploy.sh setup`/`up` warn loudly (or refuse to proceed) if `MODEL_GENERATION_PROVIDER`/`AVATAR_GENERATION_PROVIDER`/`RIGGING_PROVIDER` are still `mock` when `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE`/an explicit `--prod` flag indicates a production run; at minimum, log a `logger.warning(...)` (not `info`) in main.py whenever a provider resolves to its stub/mock branch via the default rather than an explicit, recognized value.

advisory.title: RIGGING_PROVIDER=blender is a documented, selectable option but neither worker image installs the Blender binary it requires
advisory.proof: .env.example (lines 89-92) and CLAUDE.md both document `RIGGING_PROVIDER=blender` as a valid option requiring `BLENDER_PATH` (default `blender`, main.py line 79). Neither worker/Dockerfile nor worker/Dockerfile.rigging installs a `blender` package or binary (Dockerfile.rigging's apt-get list is only `gcc g++ cmake git`). `BlenderRiggingProvider.generate()` (providers/blender_rigging_provider.py) invokes `self.blender_path` via `subprocess` — with no `blender` executable on PATH in either image, every rigging task fails at runtime with a `FileNotFoundError`-class error the first time this provider is selected in a containerized deployment. It degrades gracefully (task FAILED, not a crash), but an operator who toggles `RIGGING_PROVIDER=blender` expecting the documented behavior gets 100% rigging-task failures with no earlier validation.
advisory.fix: Either install Blender in a dedicated image for this provider (document it as container-unsupported otherwise), or remove/clearly flag `blender` as host-only/unsupported-in-Docker in .env.example and CLAUDE.md so operators don't select it expecting it to work in the shipped containers.

advisory.title: Missing .dockerignore — COPY . . bakes local dev artifacts (.venv, __pycache__, .pytest_cache, tests/) into the image when present in the build context
advisory.proof: No `.dockerignore` exists in worker/ or at the repo root (confirmed via `ls`). Both worker/Dockerfile (line 10) and worker/Dockerfile.rigging (line 17) do `COPY . .` against the `./worker` build context. On this checkout, `worker/` currently contains `.venv/`, `__pycache__/`, and `.pytest_cache/` directories alongside the real source; without an ignore file, any `docker compose build`/`./prod_deploy.sh update` run from a working tree in that state (e.g. a deploy host also used for local testing, or a CI runner that doesn't clean between steps) copies all of it into the final image layer, inflating image size and build time and risking accidental inclusion of local-only virtualenv/cache contents in what ships to production.
advisory.fix: Add a worker/.dockerignore excluding at minimum `.venv/`, `__pycache__/`, `.pytest_cache/`, `tests/`, and any `*.pyc`.

advisory.title: No resource limits anywhere in docker-compose.prod.yml — a torch-laden worker runs unbounded next to an uncapped JVM on the same host
advisory.proof: docker-compose.prod.yml's single `worker` service builds from `Dockerfile.rigging`, which installs worker/requirements.txt (torch, smplx, trimesh — unconditional deps, not feature-gated) plus libigl + robust-laplacian on top — the heaviest possible worker image, always running in prod regardless of which providers are actually enabled. Dev splits this into a base `worker` and a separate, capped `rigging-worker` (docker-compose.yml lines 105-109: `deploy: resources: limits: memory: 1G, cpus: '2.0'`), but prod has no such limit on its single merged worker, nor on any other service. The dev-only `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS: "-Xmx384m -Xms128m"` (docker-compose.yml line 43) is also absent from the prod server block, so the JVM heap sizes itself off whatever memory the host reports with no explicit ceiling. On a modest single-host production VM, a real avatar/rigging task running concurrently with normal traffic can consume unbounded memory and trigger the OOM killer against mysql/server, which (per the restart-policy finding above) will not auto-recover.
advisory.fix: Add `deploy.resources.limits` (memory/cpu) to every service in docker-compose.prod.yml sized to the target host, and re-introduce an explicit JVM heap bound for the server container.

advisory.title: No backup mechanism is wired into the production deployment tooling
advisory.proof: prod_deploy.sh's command dispatch covers setup/up/update/ssl-init/ssl-renew/health/logs/stop only — there is no `backup` or `db` subcommand, and docker-compose.prod.yml defines no backup/cron sidecar either. dev.sh does have a working pair (`db backup` runs `mysqldump -u iyae -p"${DB_PASSWORD}" iyae > backup_${timestamp}.sql`), but it targets the dev compose project and is never referenced from the prod script. If the `mysql_data` volume is lost or corrupted in production (disk failure, accidental `docker volume rm`, a bad migration), there is no documented or scripted recovery path for user accounts, orders, or Stripe payment metadata.
advisory.fix: Add a `backup`/`restore` command to prod_deploy.sh (or a scheduled mysqldump sidecar in docker-compose.prod.yml) before go-live.

advisory.title: add_header inheritance trap drops the three security headers on /uploads/, /assets/, and /_next/static
advisory.proof: nginx only inherits `add_header` directives from a parent context into a child context when the child defines none of its own. `location /uploads/` (line 38), `location /assets/` (line 44), and `location /_next/static` (line 50) each define their own `add_header Cache-Control ...`, which silently drops the server-level `X-Content-Type-Options`, `X-Frame-Options`, and `Referrer-Policy` headers (lines 13-15) for every response served from those three locations -- only `/api/` and `/` (which define no add_header of their own) actually get the security headers. `/uploads/` is exactly where designer-submitted product images land, and `server/src/main/java/com/iyae/service/FileStorageService.java` validates uploads only by the client-supplied multipart `Content-Type` header (never the actual file bytes/magic numbers) before writing the content to a `.jpg/.png/.webp` file -- so this is the one location serving attacker-influenced bytes that is missing `nosniff`. I could not fully confirm current mainstream browsers would content-sniff a `Content-Type: image/jpeg` response (nginx derives that from the `.jpg` extension via its own mime map, not from the uploader) into an HTML/script execution context, so I'm not asserting a proven XSS chain -- only the concrete, verifiable nginx misconfiguration that removes the intended defense-in-depth header exactly where it would matter most.
advisory.fix: Move the three security `add_header` directives into a reusable snippet (e.g. `include security-headers.conf;`) and include it explicitly inside /uploads/, /assets/, and /_next/static as well, so they coexist with the Cache-Control header instead of being silently discarded. Separately, make FileStorageService validate actual image bytes (e.g. via a lightweight magic-number/image-decoder check) instead of trusting the client-declared Content-Type.

advisory.title: No tuned proxy timeouts for /api/, while AI chat calls to external providers have no explicit HTTP client timeout either
advisory.proof: The /api/ location sets no `proxy_read_timeout`/`proxy_connect_timeout`/`proxy_send_timeout`, so nginx uses its compiled-in 60s defaults for every call through it, including `POST /api/chat/sessions/{id}/messages`, which synchronously calls an external AI provider (Claude/DeepSeek/MiniMax per server/CLAUDE.md). A grep of server/src/main/java/com/iyae/ai/*.java found no `timeout`/`Duration.of` configuration on those HTTP clients, so a slow provider response can run well past nginx's 60s ceiling. When that happens, nginx returns a bare 504 to the user (an opaque failure rather than a clear 'AI is slow, retry' message) while the Spring thread handling that request keeps blocking on the still-in-flight AI call; repeated slow responses under concurrent chat usage tie up request threads with no corresponding client signal.
advisory.fix: Set an explicit, generous `proxy_read_timeout`/`proxy_send_timeout` (e.g. 90-120s) scoped to /api/chat/ specifically (or /api/ generally if other calls can also be slow), and add an explicit timeout to the AI provider HTTP clients that is shorter than the nginx timeout so the server fails fast and returns a clean error/fallback instead of nginx cutting the connection first.

advisory.title: No edge-level rate or connection limiting anywhere in nginx; only a 10-route in-app allowlist is throttled
advisory.proof: Neither nginx.conf nor conf.d/default.conf contains any `limit_req_zone`/`limit_req`/`limit_conn_zone`/`limit_conn` directive (confirmed by reading both files in full) -- the edge imposes no per-IP request-rate or connection-count ceiling on any path. The only throttling anywhere in the stack is `RateLimitFilter`, an explicit allowlist of exactly 10 route patterns (login, register, forgot/reset-password-adjacent, chat POSTs, checkout, public avatar generate, avatar delete, recommended-size). Every other path -- full product catalog browse/search, and the unauthenticated static locations /assets/ and /uploads/ -- has zero rate limiting at any layer. I could not confirm this causes resource exhaustion under normal (non-adversarial) load specifically, since that depends on host sizing and real traffic volume that isn't visible from the code; the confirmed fact is the structural absence of any edge-level limiter, which stacks with the unauthenticated avatar-enumeration finding above (nothing throttles that scan either).
advisory.fix: Add `limit_req_zone`/`limit_conn_zone` in nginx.conf keyed on $binary_remote_addr with a generous global ceiling (defense-in-depth beneath the app-level limiter), and specifically rate-limit /assets/ and /uploads/ given they currently have no protection at all.

advisory.title: prod_deploy.sh health check reports Docker 'unhealthy' containers as OK
advisory.fix: Don't substring-match the human-readable Status column. Use `docker inspect --format '{{.State.Health.Status}}' <container>` and compare for an exact `healthy`, so a container whose own HEALTHCHECK is failing is reported as an error instead of OK.

advisory.title: dev.sh 'reset' wipes all Docker volumes with zero confirmation
advisory.evidence:
reset)
    docker compose -f "$COMPOSE_FILE" down -v
    echo "All data wiped."
    ;;
advisory.fix: Add the same interactive confirmation pattern already used by `db restore` (or require an explicit --yes flag) before running `down -v`, since this one command destroys the MySQL data volume and all generated 3D assets irrecoverably.

advisory.title: 'db restore' confirmation prompt doesn't validate input, so it's a no-op gate
advisory.evidence:
warn "This will overwrite the current database. Press Enter to continue or Ctrl+C to cancel."
      read -r
advisory.fix: Require the operator to type a specific confirmation token (e.g. the environment name, or literal "yes") and compare it before proceeding, instead of accepting any stdin content (including a blank line piped in non-interactively, e.g. echo | ./dev.sh db restore f.sql).

advisory.title: DB password passed as a mysqldump/mysql CLI argument (visible via ps/docker top)
advisory.evidence:
docker compose -f "$COMPOSE_FILE" exec -T mysql \
        mysqldump -u iyae -p"${DB_PASSWORD}" iyae > "$backup_file"
advisory.fix: Pass the password via the MYSQL_PWD environment variable to the exec'd process (docker compose exec -T -e MYSQL_PWD="${DB_PASSWORD}" mysql mysqldump -u iyae iyae ...) instead of -p"${DB_PASSWORD}" on argv, so it isn't visible in the container's process list for the duration of the command. The same pattern is repeated in the db restore branch (mysql -u iyae -p"${DB_PASSWORD}").

advisory.title: .env and DB backup dumps are created with default (world-readable) permissions
advisory.proof: Verified host umask is 022, so cp .env.example .env (dev.sh line 131, and the identical pattern in prod_deploy.sh's setup) produces a 644, world-readable .env with no follow-up chmod. That file ends up holding DB_PASSWORD, JWT_SECRET, ANTHROPIC/DEEPSEEK/MINIMAX/WORKER_*_API_KEY, INTERNAL_MAIL_SECRET and RESEND_API_KEY. The db backup mysqldump redirect (> "$backup_file") has the same gap — the resulting SQL dump (full user table incl. password hashes and PII) also lands world-readable in the repo working directory. Any other local account on a shared dev/build host can read both files.
advisory.fix: Add chmod 600 .env immediately after it is created/modified in both dev.sh's cmd_setup/generate_jwt_secret and prod_deploy.sh's setup/generate_jwt_secret, and chmod 600 "$backup_file" immediately after the mysqldump redirect in cmd_db backup.

advisory.title: No explicit `permissions:` block — GITHUB_TOKEN runs at repo-default scope, not least-privilege
advisory.proof: No job or workflow-level `permissions:` key exists anywhere in the file (confirmed by grep across all 293 lines). None of the current steps write to the repo/PRs/packages, so there is no live sink today, but the token inherits whatever the repository's default Actions permission setting is (which can be read-write) rather than being pinned down. If a future step is added (e.g. a PR comment step, a release step) it would silently inherit broader-than-needed scope.
advisory.fix: Add `permissions: contents: read` at the top of the workflow (the only elevated need, if any, is `actions: read`/`checks: write` for artifact upload, which does not require extra scope); add narrower per-job overrides only where a job genuinely needs more.

advisory.title: All third-party actions pinned to mutable version tags, not commit SHAs
advisory.proof: Every action in the file (actions/checkout@v4, actions/setup-node@v4, actions/setup-java@v4, actions/setup-python@v5, actions/upload-artifact@v4, gradle/actions/setup-gradle@v4) is referenced by a floating major-version tag. If any of these tags were ever repointed to a malicious commit (the tj-actions/changed-files incident in March 2025 showed this happens to real, previously-trusted actions), the next `push`-to-main or PR run would execute attacker code with whatever token/secret scope the job has, with no diff for a human to review.
advisory.fix: Pin each `uses:` to a full commit SHA with the version as a trailing comment (e.g. `actions/checkout@<sha> # v4.2.2`), and use Dependabot/Renovate to keep the pinned SHAs current.

advisory.title: No dependency, SAST, or secret-scanning job anywhere in CI
advisory.evidence:
- name: Unit tests
        working-directory: web
        run: npm run test
advisory.proof: The four jobs (web-unit, server-tests, worker-tests, playwright) only typecheck/lint/test; grepping the whole file for audit/codeql/snyk/trivy/gitleaks/bandit/safety/semgrep returns no hits. A newly-introduced vulnerable npm/pip/gradle dependency, or an accidentally committed credential, would merge to main and reach production with no automated check catching it before release.
advisory.fix: Add an `npm audit --audit-level=high` step to web-unit, a `pip-audit`/`safety` step to worker-tests, a Gradle dependency-check (or OWASP dependency-check plugin) step to server-tests, and a standalone secret-scanning job (gitleaks/trufflehog) run on every push and PR.

advisory.title: Production worker image and production Spring/nginx topology are never built or exercised by CI
advisory.evidence: run: docker compose up -d --build mysql server web
advisory.proof: Verified against docker-compose.prod.yml and worker/Dockerfile.rigging: production's `worker` service builds `worker/Dockerfile.rigging` (apt-get gcc/g++/cmake + pip-installed libigl/robust-laplacian), and production runs `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod` behind an nginx reverse proxy. The Playwright job explicitly limits the build to `mysql server web` using the dev compose file and the dev Spring profile; worker-tests installs Python deps directly via pip, never through either Dockerfile. A break in the apt/pip toolchain of Dockerfile.rigging, or a prod-profile-only misconfiguration, would not be caught by any CI job — only discovered when `prod_deploy.sh up` is run against a real deploy.
advisory.fix: Add a CI step that runs `docker compose build worker rigging-worker` (or builds Dockerfile.rigging directly) so the production worker image is validated, and consider a periodic/scheduled job that brings up docker-compose.prod.yml with SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod to catch prod-only config drift before a real release.

advisory.title: ResaleService JSON snapshot parsing swallows exceptions with no logging, silently emptying a buyer's resale eligibility and purchase-provenance checks
advisory.proof: parseSnapshot() feeds listEligibleItems() (what a buyer can resell) and findOwningOrderId() (the ownership gate createListing() relies on to accept/reject a resale listing). If any order's itemsSnapshot JSON fails to deserialize into SnapshotItem — e.g. a future field rename/type change, or a historical row written before a schema change — every call site degrades silently and identically to 'the user owns nothing': listEligibleItems returns an empty list (buyer sees 'you have nothing to resell' instead of a transient/real error) and createListing throws the ordinary user-facing 'You can only resell items you've purchased' (IllegalArgumentException), which looks exactly like a legitimate rejection rather than a parsing bug. Because there is no log statement in either catch block (unlike every analogous parse-failure handler elsewhere in the server codebase), there is also no way to detect this regression after the fact short of a user complaint.
advisory.fix: Log at warn/error with the order id and exception before returning List.of(), mirroring the sibling pattern used everywhere else in this codebase (e.g. GenerationService.extractField, AvatarService.extractField, OutfitService.parseJsonList all log a warning on parse failure). Consider surfacing a degraded-state signal (e.g. a counter/metric) rather than a bare empty list, since an empty result here is indistinguishable from 'user legitimately owns nothing.'

advisory.title: No graceful shutdown anywhere (Spring default is immediate, no stop_grace_period) and the Stripe webhook silently ACKs a session with no Order row
advisory.proof: There is no `server.shutdown: graceful` and no `spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase` in `application.yml`, `application-prod.yml` or `application-dev.yml` (grepped `shutdown|graceful` across `server/src/main/resources/` and `config/` — only `SchedulerConfig`'s `setWaitForTasksToCompleteOnShutdown(true)` exists, which covers the @Scheduled pool, not HTTP requests), and `docker-compose.prod.yml` sets no `stop_grace_period`. So `prod_deploy.sh update` → `docker compose up -d` sends SIGTERM and Tomcat drops in-flight requests at once. The costly window is `CheckoutService.initiateCheckout`: the Stripe session is created at line 131 and the `Order` row is only committed at line 151 (`txTemplate.executeWithoutResult`). A SIGTERM between the two leaves a live, payable Stripe session with no order; the buyer pays, and `fulfillPaidSession` does `orderRepository.findByStripeSessionId(session.getId()).ifPresent(...)` (line 214) — no row, no log, controller returns 200, so Stripe never retries. Money taken, no order, cart not cleared, nothing recorded. I could not confirm how long a deploy's SIGTERM window actually is in practice, but the ordering of the two writes is in the code.
advisory.fix: Set `server.shutdown: graceful` plus `spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 30s`, add `stop_grace_period: 40s` to the server service, and make the unknown-session branch of `fulfillPaidSession` log an error and return a non-2xx so Stripe retries instead of silently dropping it.

advisory.title: User email addresses are logged at INFO on every transactional email and on checkout failures
advisory.evidence: log.info("{} email sent via Resend to {}", type, toEmail);
advisory.proof: `application-prod.yml` sets `root: INFO` / `com.iyae: INFO`, so this fires for every registration and every password reset. The same pattern appears in `AuthMailService:121` (`Failed to send {} email via Resend to {}`), `CheckoutService:159/162` (`Stripe session creation failed for user {}`, with `email`), `CheckoutService:361` (`...stub order {} for user {}`, with `user.getEmail()`) and `OutfitService:93/312/428/430` (`for user={}` with `user.getEmail()`). Combined with the unrotated default `json-file` driver (no `logging:` block in either compose file), a full roster of customer email addresses accumulates indefinitely on the host and in whatever log shipper is attached later — a GDPR/PIPEDA exposure that also means anyone with `docker logs` access, including a future CI/monitoring integration, gets the customer list. I did not find passwords, tokens or body measurements being logged.
advisory.fix: Log `user.getId()` instead of the email everywhere (the `AuthService` sites already do this correctly — e.g. `AuthService:155` `for user {}` with `user.getId()`), and configure log rotation + retention on all prod containers.

advisory.title: No connection-pool, thread-pool or container resource sizing in production, and one worker container serializes all three task queues
advisory.proof: Grepping `hikari|tomcat|max-connections|threads` across `server/src/main/resources/` returns nothing, so production runs HikariCP defaults (maximumPoolSize 10, connectionTimeout 30s) behind Tomcat defaults (200 request threads) against a stock `mysql:8.0` (max_connections 151) that is given no `command:` tuning in `docker-compose.prod.yml`. Under load the 191 threads that cannot get a connection block for a full 30s before failing, which nginx (default `proxy_read_timeout 60s`) happily waits on — and the three `fixedDelay = 5000` materializer tasks plus the resale sweeper compete for the same 10 connections. Separately the prod `worker` processes model, avatar and rigging tasks sequentially in one loop (`worker/main.py:138/175/210`), so a multi-minute rigging job stalls avatar generation for every buyer in the queue; and unlike the dev `rigging-worker` (`docker-compose.yml:105-109`, 1G/2 CPU limit) the prod worker has no `deploy.resources.limits`, so a rigging OOM can push the kernel OOM killer onto MySQL. I did not load-test this, so the exhaustion point is inferred from the defaults rather than measured. The JDBC URL also disables TLS to MySQL (`useSSL=false`) — contained to the Docker network, but it means DB traffic is cleartext.
advisory.fix: Set `spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size`/`connection-timeout` and `server.tomcat.threads.max` explicitly and size them against MySQL's `max_connections`; add `proxy_connect_timeout`/`proxy_read_timeout`/`proxy_send_timeout` to the nginx `/api/` location; add memory/CPU limits to the prod worker; and split rigging into its own container in prod as the dev compose already does.

advisory.title: Paid Stripe session with no matching order is silently acknowledged
advisory.proof: `fulfillPaidSession` uses `ifPresent` with no `else`, and the controller returns 200 unconditionally, so a `checkout.session.completed` whose `stripe_session_id` has no row produces no log, no metric, and no Stripe retry. That is the correct outcome for events belonging to another environment sharing the Stripe account, but it is indistinguishable from a genuinely lost order (order row never committed after session creation, or deleted), and `orders.stripe_session_id` has no unique index (V9) to make the lookup authoritative. I could not construct a code path where the user obtains the session URL without the order row having been committed, so I am filing this as reliability/observability rather than confirmed money loss.
advisory.fix: Log at WARN (ideally with an alert metric) when a `paid` session has no matching order, and add a unique index on `orders.stripe_session_id` so the mapping is enforced by the database.

advisory.title: Webhook clears the user's whole current cart, not the purchased snapshot — items added after checkout started are silently deleted
advisory.proof: The order already carries an immutable `items_snapshot` of what was paid for, but fulfillment deletes every row in the cart. Two-things-at-once scenario: the user starts checkout in tab A, then in tab B adds two more items while the Stripe page is open; the webhook lands and wipes all cart rows, so the two unpaid items vanish with no notice. Bounded impact (lost cart state, not money), but it is silent and the data to do it correctly is already on the order.
advisory.fix: Delete only the cart rows matching the `(productId, selectedSize)` pairs in the order's `items_snapshot`, leaving anything added afterwards in place.

advisory.title: Model/avatar stale-reclaim has no attempt ceiling and can run a second generation for a task that is still live, writing the same output path
advisory.evidence:
UPDATE model_generation_tasks
                SET status = 'PENDING'
                WHERE status = 'RUNNING'
                  AND updated_at < NOW() - INTERVAL 15 MINUTE
advisory.proof: Unlike `rigging_task_queue.claim_task` (which filters `attempt_count < %s`) and `rigging_task_queue.reclaim_stale_tasks` (which fails tasks at the attempt limit), the model and avatar queues neither cap attempts on claim nor on reclaim. A task whose provider call hangs past 15 minutes is therefore returned to PENDING forever: each cycle increments `attempt_count`, re-invokes the provider (for `MODEL_GENERATION_PROVIDER=meshy` that is ~30 paid credits per attempt, indefinitely), and never reaches a terminal FAILED state the designer can retry from — `GenerationService.getStatus` reports RUNNING/PENDING indefinitely. The reclaim also does not coordinate with the live worker: the original process is still running, and both it and the new claimant write `products/{product_id}/tasks/{task_id}/preview.glb` (same task id ⇒ same path), so the first to call `complete_task` (status is RUNNING again, so the guard passes) publishes READY while the other process is still writing the same file, and the server can materialize a `GarmentAsset` pointing at a partially written GLB.
advisory.fix: Mirror the rigging queue: filter `attempt_count < MAX_ATTEMPTS` in `claim_task`, and in `reclaim_stale_tasks` move tasks at/over the limit to FAILED instead of PENDING. Include a claim token (or `attempt_count`) in the `complete_task`/`fail_task` WHERE clause so a superseded worker cannot publish, and key the output path on the attempt as well as the task id.

advisory.title: Any authenticated user can reserve (and so hide) any resale listing for 30 minutes, with no rate limit on the resale checkout path
advisory.proof: `POST /api/resale/listings/{id}/checkout` reserves before any payment intent exists, and `ResaleService.browse` only returns `ResaleStatus.LISTED`, so a reservation removes the listing from the marketplace until the 30-minute TTL sweep. `RateLimitFilter`'s rule table matches the prefix `/api/checkout` (RateLimitFilter.java:37) — it does not match `/api/resale/...` — and there is no per-user cap on concurrent reservations. One authenticated account can therefore loop over `GET /api/resale/listings` and POST a checkout for every listing, re-running every 30 minutes, to keep the entire pre-loved marketplace invisible and unbuyable. Abuse-driven rather than normal-load, hence MEDIUM.
advisory.fix: Add a `RateRule("POST", "/api/resale/listings/", "/checkout", …)` to `RateLimitFilter`, cap the number of simultaneous RESERVED listings per buyer, and shorten the reservation TTL to match the Stripe session expiry set in the fix for the TTL finding.

advisory.title: `processReadyTasks` catches per-task failures inside one shared transaction, so the per-item isolation it implies does not exist
advisory.proof: The whole batch runs in one transaction while `materializeGarmentAsset` failures are swallowed per task (`catch (Exception e) { log.error(...) }`), which reads as "one bad task is skipped". For a JPA/constraint failure raised at flush, the Hibernate session is left unusable and the commit fails, so every task already materialized in that pass is rolled back while the only log line names a single task; `SchedulerConfig` then swallows the commit error too, and the scheduler re-attempts the same batch every 5 seconds — designers' 3D assets stop appearing with no clear signal. `RiggingService.processReadyTasks` has the identical shape (RiggingService.java:169-180). I could not pin a specific input that reliably throws inside `materializeGarmentAsset` on the current schema, so this is filed as misleading error handling rather than a confirmed outage.
advisory.fix: Make the loop non-transactional and move `@Transactional` onto a per-task method invoked through the bean proxy (or `REQUIRES_NEW`), so a failure isolates to that task; additionally guard materialization with a unique constraint on `garment_assets(product_id, …)` or an existence check so a retry cannot create duplicate asset rows.

advisory.title: Guest body measurements are stored indefinitely by unauthenticated callers with no deletion path and no retention job
advisory.proof: `POST /api/public/avatar/generate` is permitAll and requires no identity. `buildInputPayload` (lines 112-134) serialises `heightCm`, `weightKg`, `waistCm` (estimated from BMI when absent, line 118-121), `chestCm`, `hipsCm`, `shoulderWidthCm` and `inseamCm` into the row's `input_payload` JSON column (V6__avatar_generation_tasks.sql declares `input_payload JSON`). Those rows are never removed: `AvatarService.deleteAvatarData` is keyed on an authenticated principal's email (`deleteAvatarData(String email)`, AvatarService.java:142, reached only via `auth.getName()` in AvatarController.java:38), and no guest can authenticate as `guest@iyae.internal` — its password is a discarded random UUID (GuestAvatarService.java:87). SchedulerConfig declares no retention or pruning task of any kind (its only jobs are task materialisation, resale reservation expiry, and weather refresh). Result: an anonymous visitor who tries the landing-page avatar has their body measurements written to a production table permanently, with no self-service deletion, no admin tooling, and no expiry. I could not confirm any out-of-band retention process (cron, DB event) — none exists in the repository.
advisory.fix: Add a scheduled purge of `avatar_generation_tasks` rows belonging to the guest sentinel user older than a short, documented TTL (hours, not days), deleting the on-disk output alongside — `AvatarService.deleteAvatarFiles` already has the recursive-delete helper to reuse. State the TTL in the guest try-on UI.

advisory.title: Registration requires agreeing to a Terms and Privacy Policy that does not exist anywhere in the product
advisory.evidence: I agree to {BRAND.name}'s Terms and Privacy Policy.
advisory.proof: The consent checkbox is rendered as plain text with no link target. There is no `/privacy` or `/terms` route in `web/app/` (the directory listing contains neither), no file matching `*privacy*` or `*terms*` anywhere outside node_modules, and this is the single occurrence of the words "Privacy Policy" across web/app, web/components and web/lib. So a user collecting-consent flow asks 18-30 year olds to accept documents they cannot read, for a product that stores body measurements, gender identity, age range and a derived 3D body mesh. Separately, no surface discloses data handling at the point of collection: a grep for `third.party|we store|consent|anthropic|claude|deepseek|minimax|data deletion` across web/app/profile and web/components/profile returns nothing, and the avatar page's privacy copy is limited to "Permanently removes your 3D avatar and measurements." (web/app/profile/avatar/page.tsx:465).
advisory.fix: Ship a privacy policy and terms page (or external links) and wire the checkbox label to them, covering at minimum: what body measurements are collected, that a 3D body mesh is derived and stored, retention periods, and the deletion controls available. Add a one-line disclosure at the measurement-entry and avatar-generation points of collection.

advisory.title: No fast test validates that the JPA entity mappings match the real Flyway migrations (ddl-auto=validate in prod)
advisory.evidence:
hibernate:
      ddl-auto: create-drop
    ...
  flyway:
    enabled: false
advisory.proof: Every server test (including `IyaeApplicationTests`, which explicitly excludes `DataSourceAutoConfiguration`/`HibernateJpaAutoConfiguration`/`FlywayAutoConfiguration`) and every `@DataJpaTest` (e.g. `ResaleListingRepositoryDataJpaTest`) runs against H2 with Hibernate auto-generating the schema from entities and Flyway turned off — so none of them ever load the real V1-V21 migration SQL. Production uses `ddl-auto: validate` against Flyway-applied migrations (server/src/main/resources/application.yml:9), so a column type/nullability mismatch only surfaces as a boot failure once deployed. CLAUDE.md documents a real near-miss of exactly this class of bug (`PasswordResetTokenRepository.consumeToken` assigning CURRENT_TIMESTAMP to an Instant, "breaks full JPA bootstrap"). The only thing in CI that would currently catch a repeat is the Playwright job's `docker compose up` + health-check retry loop, which gives a generic 5-minute timeout with no indication the root cause is a schema mismatch.
advisory.fix: Add a dedicated, fast test (or Gradle task) that boots Spring Boot against a real database (e.g. Testcontainers MySQL, or H2 with Flyway enabled and ddl-auto=validate) so an entity<->migration mismatch fails in the 20-minute `server-tests` CI job instead of only in the 60-minute Playwright job's opaque "API never became healthy" timeout.

advisory.title: StripeWebhookController's "invalid signature" test exercises a code path the real service never takes

advisory.title: Catalog free-text search (`q`) uses a leading-wildcard LIKE with no usable index
advisory.proof: A `LIKE '%term%'` predicate cannot use a B-tree index in MySQL regardless of what's indexed (V2__indexes_and_constraints.sql only adds idx_products_status_category and idx_products_status_created, neither of which helps a leading-wildcard scan on name/description). Every search request therefore does a filtered scan of all PUBLISHED rows after the status predicate narrows it. At the current seeded scale (36 products) this is invisible; I could not confirm the production catalog size, so I can't say this currently breaks anything — flagging as a scalability gap that will show up as catalog size grows into the thousands, on the shop's search box specifically.
advisory.fix: Add a MySQL FULLTEXT index on products(name, description) and switch the `q` branch to MATCH ... AGAINST, or move search to a dedicated search index if the catalog is expected to grow past a few thousand PUBLISHED rows.

advisory.title: 3D-generation/avatar/rigging worker is a single serial process — no horizontal scale-out configured
advisory.evidence:
task = queue.claim_task()
            if task is not None:
                processed_any = True
                task_id = task["id"]
                product_id = task["product_id"]
                logger.info(f"Claimed model task {task_id} for product {product_id}")
advisory.proof: Each poll loop iteration claims and fully processes at most one model-generation task, one avatar task, and one rigging task, each synchronously end-to-end (network call to the provider, GLB validation, DB write) before looping again — there is no concurrency within the process. docker-compose.yml and docker-compose.prod.yml both declare exactly one `worker` service instance (the separate `rigging-worker` is also a single instance, gated behind the `rigging` profile). If a provider call takes on the order of a minute, 10 designers triggering generation within the same window queue strictly serially: the 10th request's task sits PENDING while the prior 9 complete, so its status poll (GenerationStatusController, 5s interval per web/lib/hooks/useGenerationStatus.ts) could show PENDING for several minutes. The underlying claim mechanism (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED in worker/task_queue.py) is already safe for multiple replicas, so this is a deployment-topology gap rather than a code defect — I could not confirm how many designers submit generation requests concurrently in production, so this is flagged as a latency/availability risk under burst load rather than a confirmed outage.
advisory.fix: Run the `worker` service with multiple replicas (docker-compose supports it since task_queue.claim_task already uses `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, which is safe for concurrent claimers) when generation volume grows, or document the current single-instance ceiling so it's a known tradeoff rather than a surprise under a traffic spike.

advisory.title: Product price and resale asking price have no upper bound before hitting a DECIMAL(10,2) column
advisory.proof: A designer calling POST /api/designer/products (or a buyer calling POST /api/resale/listings) with price=100000000000 passes @DecimalMin(0.01) validation (no @DecimalMax exists) and reaches Hibernate, which attempts to persist a value that exceeds DECIMAL(10,2)'s range. This surfaces as a DataIntegrityViolationException, which GlobalExceptionHandler.handleDataIntegrityViolation (server/src/main/java/com/iyae/config/GlobalExceptionHandler.java) maps to HTTP 409 'Data conflict: please retry' — a response that tells the user to retry an operation that will never succeed, instead of the clean 400 'Price must be at most X' that @DecimalMax would have produced. The matching client forms (web/components/ProductForm.tsx:251 `min="0" step="0.01"`, web/components/ResaleListingForm.tsx:82 `min="0.01" step="0.01"`) have no upper bound either, so nothing stops this value from being typed.
advisory.fix: Add @DecimalMax(value = "99999999.99") (or a sane business-level cap) to price in CreateProductRequest/UpdateProductRequest and to askingPrice in CreateResaleListingRequest/UpdateResaleListingRequest, matching the DECIMAL(10,2) column width (`server/src/main/resources/db/migration/V1__baseline_schema.sql:47`, `Product.java:35` precision=10/scale=2) and the resale_listings.asking_price column (`V16__resale_listings.sql:11`).

advisory.title: Product name/category/currency have no @Size guard before VARCHAR(255/100/3) columns
advisory.proof: A DESIGNER calling POST /api/designer/products directly (bypassing the UI's unbounded <Input> at web/components/ProductForm.tsx:218-226, which also has no maxLength) with a 1000-character name passes @NotBlank and reaches the DB insert against products.name VARCHAR(255). In MySQL's default strict mode this raises a data-too-long error, which Spring's exception translator reports as DataIntegrityViolationException -> mapped by GlobalExceptionHandler to HTTP 409 'Data conflict: please retry' rather than a clear 400 telling the designer the name is too long.
advisory.fix: Add @Size(max = 255) to name, @Size(max = 100) to category, and @Size(max = 3) to currency in both CreateProductRequest and UpdateProductRequest to match products.name VARCHAR(255), products.category VARCHAR(100), and products.currency VARCHAR(3) (server/src/main/resources/db/migration/V1__baseline_schema.sql:45-48).

advisory.title: Guest avatar generation shares one global user identity — cross-session avatar overwrite + unauthenticated IDOR on task status
advisory.proof: GuestAvatarController exposes `POST /api/public/avatar/generate` and `GET /api/public/avatar/status/{taskId}` fully unauthenticated (`/api/public/**` is `permitAll()` in SecurityConfig.java:48). Every call to GuestAvatarService.getOrCreateGuestUser() (lines 81-89) returns the SAME single `User` row keyed by `brandProperties.guestEmail()` — there is one guest identity shared by every anonymous visitor on the server. Consequently every `AvatarGenerationTask` created by `generateForGuest()` has the identical `user_id`, and the 'ownership' check at line 65 (`task.getUser().getId().equals(guest.getId())`) is vacuously true for every task that has ever been created by any anonymous visitor — it never rejects anyone. Worse, the worker writes the generated avatar to a path keyed by that same shared `user_id`: `worker/providers/smplx_provider.py:313-315,362` (`output_dir = .../avatars/{user_id}`; `glb_url: /assets/avatars/{user_id}/avatar.glb`) and `smplx_stub_provider.py:234-256` do the same. Concrete production failure: Guest A submits measurements and gets task #101 (owner = shared guest id G). Guest B, an unrelated anonymous visitor minutes or hours later, submits different measurements and gets task #102 (owner is also G). B's generation completes and the worker overwrites `avatars/G/avatar.glb` with B's body mesh. A's own, already-completed result is now permanently destroyed (silent data loss), and if A polls `GET /api/public/avatar/status/101` again (or the frontend re-fetches the cached URL), A is served B's generated 3D body avatar as if it were their own. Separately, because the ownership check never actually discriminates between visitors, anyone can sequentially enumerate the auto-increment `taskId` (`@GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)` on AvatarGenerationTask) with zero authentication and read the status/result/error of every guest avatar task the server has ever processed. No privileged precondition, no credentials, and no attacker sophistication beyond incrementing an integer are required — ordinary concurrent use of the advertised 'try without an account' flow reproduces the corruption on its own.
advisory.fix: Stop collapsing every anonymous visitor onto one shared `guest@iyae.internal` User row. Either (a) mint a per-session disposable identity (and have the worker key the output path by `task_id`, not `user_id`), or (b) at minimum change the SMPL-X/stub providers to write to `avatars/guest/{taskId}/avatar.glb` instead of `avatars/{user_id}/avatar.glb` so concurrent anonymous generations cannot collide, and bind `GuestAvatarStatusResponse` access to a per-generation secret (e.g. an opaque token returned from /generate) rather than a same-row comparison that is always true.
verifierSummary: [reachable] isReal=true conf=0.9 sev->HIGH: REACHABLE IN PRODUCTION — could not refute. Evidence read: SecurityConfig.java:48 has `.requestMatchers("/api/public/**").permitAll()`; GuestAvatarController is `@RequestMapping("/api/public/avatar")` with no @Profile/feature gate, so both /generate and /status/{taskId} are unauthenticated in every profile. nginx/conf.d/default.conf:27 proxies `location /api/` to the server in the ACTIVE (uncommented) prod server block. GuestAvatarService.java:81-93 resolves one single User row by brandProperties.guestEmail() (application.yml:47 -> guest@iyae.internal), so the line-65 ownership check compares a guest task's owner against that same constant and can never reject it. worker/main.py:175-183 + avatar_task_queue.py claim ANY pending row and pass its user_id to provider.generate(); both providers key the output path on user_id — smplx_provider.py:313/362 and smplx_stub_provider.py:234/256 (`avatars/{user_id}/avatar.glb`). docker-compose.prod.yml:68 defaults AVATAR_GENERATION_PROVIDER=mock, which selects SmplxStubProvider — i.e. the colliding path exists on the DEFAULT prod provider, there is no setting that avoids it. nginx default.conf:41-45 serves `/assets/` straight off the shared volume with `expires 7d; immutable`, so the one shared file is world-readable and aggressively cached. RateLimitFilter.java:38 throttles only POST /generate; the status GET is unthrottled. Corroborating detail the finding missed: AvatarService.materializeAvatar (214-227) scopes its "latest READY" guard to the task's user, so with every guest on one row only the newest guest task materializes while older ones stay READY and still return the shared URL — and the method already special-cases isGuest at line 233, showing the shared identity was known but the output-path collision was not handled. SEVERITY CORRECTED CRITICAL -> HIGH on three measured overstatements. (1) grep over all of web/ for `public/avatar`, `api/public` and `guest` finds NO caller — the "advertised try-without-an-account flow" is not wired into the shipped frontend, so "ordinary concurrent use reproduces the corruption on its own" is false; reaching it needs a deliberate direct API client. (2) The IDOR/enumeration discloses essentially nothing: GuestAvatarStatusResponse is (taskId, status, glbUrl, errorMessage) with no measurements and no identity, and glbUrl is the SAME constant string for every guest task. (3) Authenticated users are NOT exposed via this path — for a real user's task the guest-id comparison is false and the request is correctly rejected, so no account-linked avatar or data leaks here. The real harm that remains is genuine: one anonymous visitor's generated body mesh overwrites another's at a public URL, destroying the first result and serving B's body mesh to A — unauthenticated cross-session data bleed plus silent data loss, on identity-less self-submitted artifacts, currently shielded only by the absence of a UI caller (a control that disappears the moment the flow is wired). That is HIGH, not CRITICAL. Uncertainty did not clear anything: I found no dev-only gate, disabled flag, unmounted route or dead code.

[mitigated] isReal=true conf=0.85 sev->MEDIUM: I looked for a mitigation at every layer the lens names and found none that closes the hole. The mechanism is real, but the blast radius is far smaller than the finding claims, so CRITICAL is wrong.

WHAT I VERIFIED AS TRUE
- `/Users/jadyn/Development/IYAE/server/src/main/java/com/iyae/config/SecurityConfig.java:48` is `.requestMatchers("/api/public/**").permitAll()`, and `GuestAvatarController` is mapped at `/api/public/avatar` with `POST /generate` + `GET /status/{taskId}`. No `@PreAuthorize` on it (only AdminController/AnalyticsController use method security), no interceptor, and `nginx/conf.d/default.conf` proxies all of `/api/` without any rule on `/api/public`. Unauthenticated reachability confirmed.

advisory.title: Admin moderation lock (moderation_locked) is not enforced on the designer DELETE path
advisory.proof: AdminModerationService.setProductStatus sets moderationLocked=true whenever an admin forces a product to ARCHIVED, with the explicit intent (its own comment) that this 'durably locks the listing so the owning designer cannot silently republish it'. ProductService.updateProduct enforces that lock for the status-change path (throws AccessDeniedException, ProductService.java:197-200) and that behavior is unit-tested (ProductServiceTest#updateProduct_moderationLocked_rejectsStatusChangeOutOfArchived). deleteProduct has no equivalent check anywhere -- grep for moderationLocked/isModerationLocked in the whole server tree shows exactly one read site (ProductService.java:197) and one write site (AdminModerationService.java:76); deleteProduct never reads the flag. Once an admin archives a product for a policy violation (counterfeit, IP infringement, prohibited content), the owning designer -- who still passes the ownership check in requireOwnedProduct -- can call DELETE /api/designer/products/{id} and permanently erase the row. Because products.id has ON DELETE CASCADE from reviews, product_size_measurements, cart_items, model_generation_tasks, rigging_tasks and saved_products (V1/V7/V12/V21 migrations), this also silently destroys buyer-authored reviews and wishlist entries for that product, not just the designer's own data, and wipes every trace of the admin's moderation action, after which the designer can immediately re-POST an identical listing with a clean slate. ProductServiceTest's delete suite (deleteProduct_ownerCanDelete, _nonOwner_, _nonexistentProduct_) never sets moderationLocked on the fixture, confirming this path was never exercised -- unlike the documented, deliberately-tested non-status-edit allowance.
advisory.fix: In deleteProduct, throw AccessDeniedException when product.isModerationLocked() is true, mirroring the existing updateProduct check; only an admin un-archive (AdminModerationService.setProductStatus) should be able to clear the lock before the designer can delete or republish.

advisory.title: Uncaught ClassCastException from a type-confused [GENERATE_OUTFIT] payload 500s the chat turn and orphans the user's message
advisory.proof: extractGenerateOutfitRequest (ChatService.java:256-266) deserializes the AI's [GENERATE_OUTFIT] JSON into Map<String,Object> and then does `List<String> colorPalette = (List<String>) parsed.get("colorPalette")` (line 263) — an unchecked generic cast that, due to type erasure, does NOT throw even if the array contains non-string elements (e.g. the model emits {"colorPalette":["black",5]}, which Jackson turns into a List<Object> holding String "black" and Integer 5). The malformed GenerateOutfitRequest is returned successfully (no exception is caught at line 267's catch block, since none was thrown yet). It then flows, un-wrapped, into `outfitService.generateOutfitAnonymous(parsedOutfitRequest)` at ChatService.java:187 — unlike the very next step (persistOutfit at lines 193-198), this call has no try/catch. Inside OutfitService.buildOutfitResponse -> scoreProduct, the code does `for (String requestColor : requestColors)` over the mistyped list; the compiler-inserted checkcast throws ClassCastException at that point, uncaught, and propagates out of ChatService.sendMessage to GlobalExceptionHandler's catch-all RuntimeException handler, returning a generic 500. By that time, the user's ChatMessage was already saved (Step 1, chatMessageRepository.save(userMessage) at line 148) in its own transaction, so the turn ends with the user's message persisted and no assistant reply ever recorded, while the client sees an opaque 500. This requires no attacker — any AI provider occasionally emitting a non-string element in colorPalette (budget providers like DeepSeek/MiniMax are explicitly supported and not schema-constrained by the API) reproduces it, and a user who deliberately prompt-injects the model into emitting such a payload can trigger it at will.
advisory.fix: Wrap the outfitService.generateOutfitAnonymous(...) call in the same try/catch style already used for persistOutfit (log and fall back to null/explanatory message), and/or validate GenerateOutfitRequest.colorPalette element types (filter to actual Strings) inside extractGenerateOutfitRequest before returning, so a malformed AI payload degrades to 'no outfit generated' instead of 500ing the whole turn.

advisory.title: resale_listings FK to products/users has no ON DELETE action — product deletion permanently fails once an item is ever resold
advisory.evidence:
FOREIGN KEY (seller_id) REFERENCES users(id),
    FOREIGN KEY (product_id) REFERENCES products(id),
advisory.proof: A designer calls DELETE /api/designer/products/{id}. ProductService.deleteProduct(email,id) does `productRepository.delete(product)` with no check for resale_listings (server/src/main/java/com/iyae/service/ProductService.java:210-214). If that product was ever the subject of a buyer resale listing (any status — DRAFT/LISTED/RESERVED/SOLD/CANCELLED all leave a row), InnoDB's default RESTRICT action on this FK rejects the DELETE with a FK-constraint violation. Spring wraps it as DataIntegrityViolationException, which GlobalExceptionHandler.handleDataIntegrityViolation (server/src/main/java/com/iyae/config/GlobalExceptionHandler.java:63-72) maps to HTTP 409 'Data conflict: please retry'. Retrying is pointless — the constraint can never be satisfied while the resale_listings row exists, and nothing in the app lets a designer or admin remove it via the API. The product becomes permanently undeletable, and the designer sees a message that falsely implies retry will help.
advisory.fix: Add an explicit, friendly guard in ProductService.deleteProduct (check for existing resale_listings referencing the product and raise a clear 409/422 with an actionable message) — or, if the product should remain deletable once resold, change the FK to ON DELETE SET NULL/CASCADE-with-archival semantics instead of silently relying on RESTRICT-via-omission. Also audit the symmetric seller_id FK (same file, line 19) for the same gap against any future user-deletion feature.

advisory.title: CartProvider refetches /api/cart with no request sequencing — a stale response can overwrite a fresher cart, silently reverting items the user just added/removed
advisory.proof: refreshCart is recreated (and the effect reruns) every time the `user` object's reference changes — and auth-context.tsx always hands out a brand-new user object on login/register/updateProfile/refreshUser (confirmed in auth-context.tsx:75-104), even when the underlying account is unchanged. There is no AbortController and no 'is this still the latest request' guard, so two /api/cart GETs can be in flight at once (e.g. user logs in on a slow connection, then edits their profile via the SiteHeader menu — which calls `refreshUser` — before the first GET resolves). If the older request resolves after the newer one, its `.then` calls setFetchedItems with the stale snapshot, overwriting the correct, newer cart — and since `fetchedForUserId` is set to the same user id either way, the mismatch guard on line 115-117 does not catch it. Concretely: cart shows 3 items after an add, then an older, slower /api/cart response lands and the cart silently drops back to 1 item on screen. web/app/checkout/page.tsx:78-82 derives its displayed subtotal/order-summary from this same serverItems state, so the checkout page can show the shopper fewer items/a lower total than what the actual server-side cart (and therefore what Stripe is told to charge) contains.
advisory.fix: Guard refreshCart against out-of-order responses: track a monotonically increasing request id (or an AbortController keyed per-call) and only commit setFetchedItems/setFetchedForUserId if the resolving call is still the latest one issued — the same pattern already used in web/components/dashboard/OrdersPanel.tsx and documented as the fix for the identical bug class elsewhere in this codebase (useRiggingStatus, products/page.tsx).

advisory.proof: Confirmed by reading the installed library source: useGLTF (web/node_modules/@react-three/drei/core/Gltf.js:27) is useLoader(GLTFLoader, path, ...), and useLoader (web/node_modules/@react-three/fiber/.../events-*.js, function useLoader) calls suspend-react's suspend(fn, [loader, ...keys]) with no lifespan config. suspend-react's cache (web/node_modules/suspend-react/index.cjs.js) is `const globalCache = []` -- a plain array whose entries are only removed by an explicit clear() call or a configured lifespan timeout, neither of which useGLTF/useLoader ever supplies. A repo-wide search for useGLTF.clear/useLoader.clear/.dispose( across web/components and web/lib returns zero matches -- nothing in this app ever evicts an entry. Every distinct GLB URL loaded by GarmentModel/AvatarModel/BoundGarmentModel (this file) and PlacedModel (web/components/ARViewer.tsx:81) therefore keeps its full decoded THREE.js scene graph (geometries + uploaded GPU textures) resident for the entire SPA session (this app is 100% client-rendered, so there is no full page reload between routes per web/CLAUDE.md). A shopper who visits outfits/[id]/view for several different outfits, or taps the inline 'Try on' toggle on several OutfitCard feed posts, or browses the style-lab -> outfits -> try-on flow for a while, accumulates one cache entry per distinct product/avatar GLB -- each a few MB of geometry + texture data -- with none ever freed. On a memory-constrained mobile browser (iOS Safari in particular enforces a hard per-tab WebGL/GPU memory ceiling), this is a realistic path to a WebGL context loss or a tab reload after normal, not pathological, browsing -- exactly the 'crashes a mobile browser after a few navigations' scenario this audit asked about.
advisory.fix: Call useGLTF.clear(url) (or useLoader.clear(GLTFLoader, url)) when a viewer unmounts or when its url/avatarUrl/garmentUrls props change to a different value no longer needed, or pass useLoader's lifespan option so stale entries age out automatically. At minimum, cap how many distinct GLB URLs can be live in the cache at once on pages that render many viewers in a session (outfits/[id]/view, OutfitCard's inline try-on).

advisory.title: No error boundary around the 3D canvas on the public /ar-visualization page
advisory.proof: SmartARViewer routes to AvatarViewer/ARViewer, both of which call useGLTF inside a <Suspense> boundary -- a load failure (the static asset returning non-200, a truncated/corrupt GLB, or WebGL context creation throwing on an unsupported browser) throws synchronously during render. Suspense only catches thrown promises; a thrown error propagates to the nearest React error boundary. advisory.fix: Wrap <SmartARViewer glbUrls={[DEMO_GLB_URL]} /> in <ViewerErrorBoundary fallback={...}> the same way outfits/[id]/ar and OutfitBuilderPreview do, so a bad asset degrades to a static fallback instead of taking down the whole page.
