ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
advisory.proof: The final stage never adds/switches to a non-root `USER`, so the JVM process runs as root inside the container — a defense-in-depth gap if any future RCE/arbitrary-file-write vulnerability is found in this app or a dependency. The ENTRYPOINT also bakes in no JVM heap bound (e.g. -XX:MaxRAMPercentage) of its own; the repo's only memory cap (`JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS: "-Xmx384m -Xms128m"`) is supplied externally by docker-compose.yml and is documented in root CLAUDE.md as "dev docker-compose only" — docker-compose.prod.yml sets no JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS and no container memory limit for the server service, so in production the JVM's default container-aware heap ergonomics are the only guard against a memory spike/leak taking down the shared host alongside MySQL/web/nginx. There is also no `HEALTHCHECK` instruction in the image itself (health checks exist only in the compose files), so the image has no self-contained liveness signal if run under an orchestrator that doesn't supply its own probe.
advisory.fix: Add a dedicated non-root `USER` in the final stage (chown the jar accordingly); set a conservative default heap bound directly in the ENTRYPOINT (e.g. `ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0", "-jar", "app.jar"]`) so the image is safe even without an external JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS; add a `HEALTHCHECK` instruction as a baked-in fallback.

advisory.title: ImageUploader: stale upload can overwrite a newer selection, and an in-flight object URL can leak on unmount
advisory.proof: There is no guard against a second file being selected (via click or drag) while the first `uploadImage()` call is still in flight — `handleFile` has no request-id/AbortController. If the first upload resolves after the second has already started, its `.then` still runs and calls `onUpload(uploadedUrl1)` + `setPreviewUrl(uploadedUrl1)`, silently reverting the form's imageUrl back to the first (stale) file even though the user had already moved on to a second selection. Separately, the `URL.createObjectURL(file)` object URL is only revoked inside the same `handleFile` call's success/catch paths — if the component unmounts while the upload promise is still pending (e.g. the designer navigates away from the new/edit product page mid-upload), that blob URL is never revoked and leaks for the life of the SPA session.
advisory.fix: Track a request id/ref (or AbortController) per call and ignore a `handleFile` invocation's result if a newer one has started since; revoke the object URL (or at least guard the `setPreviewUrl`/`onUpload` calls) in a cleanup path if the component unmounts mid-upload.

advisory.title: Stale per-device wishlist cache can silently resurrect a product the user removed on another device
advisory.proof: Sign in on device A, save product X (write(X) to localStorage AND POST /api/saved-products). Leave device A signed in (JWT TTL 24h, no further sync — hydration is memoised 'at most once per page load' and nothing re-runs it while the tab stays open). On device B, unsave X (server list becomes []). Back on device A, open a new tab or reload: module state resets, `hydrate()` runs, `serverIds=[]`, but the stale localStorage cache still has `[X]` from before — so `localOnly=[X]`. The code writes the union to cache (line 113, UI shows X saved again) and then calls `savedProductsApi.save(X)` (line 116) to 'replay' it, which recreates the saved_products row on the server — silently undoing the user's own explicit unsave from device B with no error, confirmation, or way to detect it happened. The code has no timestamp/tombstone to distinguish 'added while genuinely offline' from 'stale cache that diverged because the item was removed elsewhere', which the function's own doc comment (lines 86-91) does not address — it only reasons about additions missing locally, not about resurrecting a remote removal.
advisory.fix: Track saves/removes with a per-id timestamp or version (or at minimum a tombstone set for recent local removals) so hydrate() can tell 'never synced, must push' apart from 'synced previously, diverged because of a later server-side removal'. At minimum, stop treating every local-only id as a pending write on every hydrate() call — only replay ids that were added while `!hasAuthToken()` was true (i.e. genuinely offline), not ids left over from a previous session.

So guest-owned rows only exist if someone calls the API directly. This does not refute reachability (an attacker can call it), but it means there is no stream of victim rows to harvest.

advisory.title: Cart read/write path N+1 loads Product per line item (no JOIN FETCH, no batch-fetch)
advisory.proof: CartItem.product is `@ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)` (server/src/main/java/com/iyae/entity/CartItem.java:27-29) and CartItemRepository.findByCartId (repository/CartItemRepository.java:10) is a plain derived query with no fetch join. CartResponse.CartItemResponse.from(item) then calls item.getProduct().getName()/.getPrice()/.getMedia()/.getCurrency() for every item — each a separate lazy-load SELECT, since application.yml sets no hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size. buildResponse is the tail of getCart, addItem, updateItem, AND removeItem, so every single cart read or mutation (not just GET /api/cart) pays 1 + N queries for an N-item cart: a shopper with 8 items in the cart generates 9 round trips per cart view, and the same 9 on every add/update/remove click. This is the literal shopping-cart hot path and scales with concurrent shoppers x items-per-cart.
advisory.fix: Add a JOIN FETCH query (e.g. `@Query("SELECT ci FROM CartItem ci JOIN FETCH ci.product WHERE ci.cart.id = :cartId") List<CartItem> findByCartIdFetchProduct(Long cartId)`) and use it in buildResponse, or set `spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size` so the lazy Product loads coalesce into one IN(...) query.

CartResponse.CartItemResponse.from() dereferences item.getProduct() five times (getId/getName/getPrice/getMedia/getCurrency), initializing the proxy once per distinct product. I grepped server/src/main/ for `default_batch_fetch_size` and `BatchSize` — zero hits; application.yml sets no such property and application-prod.yml overrides only show-sql + logging levels, so prod adds no batching. server/build.gradle.kts contains no hibernate/cache/ehcache/jcache dependency at all, so there is no second-level cache to absorb the loads. CartService.buildResponse really is the tail of all four of getCart/addItem/updateItem/removeItem. So 1 + N(distinct products) per cart read AND per mutation is accurate (addItem is 1 cheaper, since requireProduct already put that one product in the persistence context).

PRODUCTION REACHABILITY: SecurityConfig.java has no /api/cart matcher and terminates at line 52 with `.anyRequest().authenticated()`, so the cart endpoints are reachable by any authenticated user (explicitly in scope). docker-compose.prod.yml:36 sets SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: prod, which per application-prod.yml changes nothing relevant. Not gated by a flag, profile, or unmounted component. Found no mitigating or unreachability evidence of any kind.

N is bounded by distinct cart lines (realistically single digits; practically capped by the 36-product seeded catalogue x sizes), and each extra load is an intra-Docker primary-key SELECT, i.e. single-digit extra ms for an 8-item cart. The one factor arguing it up is call frequency (every page load per signed-in user, since the provider sits in the root layout), which makes MEDIUM defensible but not HIGH. Separately, the filed category `correctness` is wrong — this is a performance finding, consistent with its x-perf reporter. Proposed fix is sound; the default_batch_fetch_size variant is cheaper and would address the same shape elsewhere.

That is a MEDIUM efficiency defect on a hot path, not a HIGH, and the filed category "correctness" should be "efficiency". advisory.title: Root error.tsx has no escape route, and since every page renders its own SiteHeader, a crash anywhere strands the user with no navigation
advisory.evidence:
Something went wrong

...
advisory.proof: SiteHeader (containing all nav links: home/products/cart/orders/etc.) is rendered inline inside each page.tsx (confirmed present in 35 of 44 pages, e.g. app/checkout/page.tsx:132, app/products/[id]/page.tsx:260, app/cart/page.tsx:226) rather than in app/layout.tsx, which only wraps children in AuthProvider/CartProvider/ThemeProvider with no header. Next.js mounts app/error.tsx as the boundary replacing a crashed page's whole render tree, including that page's own SiteHeader. So if, say, checkout/page.tsx throws on a render-time null-reference (e.g. a malformed cart/shipping-option payload), the entire screen becomes error.tsx's generic panel: no header, no nav links, and the ONLY control is 'Try Again' (reset()), which simply re-renders the exact same crashing tree. If the trigger is deterministic (bad data that will reload the same way), the user has zero way to navigate to any other page except editing the URL bar by hand or using the browser back button — a real production dead end for a core flow like checkout.
advisory.fix: Add a 'Go to homepage' (or 'Back to shop') Link to app/error.tsx mirroring not-found.tsx's recovery links, and/or move SiteHeader into app/layout.tsx so navigation survives a page-level crash.

1. `/Users/jadyn/Development/IYAE/web/app/error.tsx` is exactly as quoted: a `"use client"` boundary whose only interactive control is `<button onClick={reset}>Try Again</button>`. No `next/link` import, no href, no anchor anywhere in the file.

There is no `SiteHeader` and no nav of any kind in the layout.
3. `SiteHeader` is rendered inline by 35 of the 44 `page.tsx` files (verified by grep; e.g. `web/app/checkout/page.tsx:132` is literally `<SiteHeader variant="app" />` inside the page's own return). The 9 without it are home + the auth/verify pages. So the header is unambiguously page-level, and Next.js replaces the crashed page segment (header included) with `error.tsx`.
4. `find web/app -name "layout.tsx"` returns only the root layout, and `find` for `error.tsx`/`global-error.tsx` returns only `web/app/error.tsx`. So this single boundary is the fallback for all 44 routes, and there is no `global-error.tsx` at all.
5. `web/app/not-found.tsx` does carry two recovery `<Link>`s ("Go Home", "Browse Products"), confirming the claimed inconsistency.

Not dev-gated: `docker-compose.prod.yml` (`web:` service, lines 84-96) builds `./web` with the same `web/Dockerfile`, and `web/next.config.ts` is a plain `output: "standalone"` build. `error.tsx` is a Next.js convention file compiled into the production bundle. - `FloatingAIStylist` is a *sibling* of `{children}` in the root layout, so it survives the error boundary. why:

Proof read from the installed router, not from memory:
- node_modules/next/dist/client/components/layout-router.js (OuterLayoutRouter) comments: "The 'state' key of a segment is the one passed to React — it represents the identity of the UI tree. Whenever the state key changes, the tree is recreated and the state is reset." The child subtree is rendered with React key `stateKey` (`}, stateKey)`).
- node_modules/next/dist/client/components/router-reducer/create-router-cache-key.js: for a dynamic segment the key is `${segment[0]}|${segment[1]}|${segment[2]}`, i.e. the PARAM VALUE is part of the state key (`id|1|d` vs `id|2|d`).
- node_modules/next/dist/server/app-render/create-component-tree.js:462 creates a LayoutRouter for every parallel-route slot of every tree level, so `[id]` is inside a keyed boundary even though web/app/orders has no layout.tsx or template.tsx (only web/app/layout.tsx exists).
- node_modules/next/dist/client/components/bfcache-state-manager.js: MAX_BF_CACHE_ENTRIES = __NEXT_CACHE_COMPONENTS ? 3 : 1; web/next.config.ts does not enable cacheComponents, so the old param's subtree is dropped outright rather than kept state-preserving in a hidden <Activity>.
- Next 16.2.6's own shipped docs (docs/01-app/.../template.md): "They remount when that segment (including its dynamic params) changes... Any Client Component inside the template will reset its state on navigation... Effects like useEffect will re-synchronize as the component remounts", with /blog/first-post -> /blog/second-post as the worked example.

Consequences for each claim: (1) the "deterministic repro (no network race needed)" does not reproduce — /orders/A (error) -> /orders/B mounts a FRESH instance with order=null, loading=true, error=null, so no stale banner stacks above B's details; (2) "renders order A's full detail view for the duration of B's request" is false — B starts on the skeleton; (3) "order A's data can persist under order B's URL" is false — A's instance is unmounted and its .then(setOrder) is a silent no-op in React 19. The missing AbortController is wasted bandwidth, not a correctness bug. Separately, nothing in the tree links order->order (the page's only outbound link is /orders, grep-confirmed), so even the typed-URL path passes through /orders, which unmounts the segment.

Residual, NOT what was filed and not HIGH: the effect can re-run within one instance when the `user` object identity changes (refreshUser via ProfileSettingsDialog, which this page's own SiteHeader mounts — SiteHeader.tsx:391). A transient failure followed by a profile save would refetch the SAME order id and leave the old banner above correct data — cosmetic, right order, no wrong-order data. WHAT IS FALSE: the premise "Because /orders/[id] is one component instance reused across param changes". In Next.js 16.2.6 the segment subtree's React key embeds the param value, so a param change remounts the page with fresh useState:
- web/node_modules/next/dist/client/components/layout-router.js:462-464 says it outright: "The 'state' key of a segment is the one passed to React — it represents the identity of the UI tree. Whenever the state key changes, the tree is recreated and the state is reset."
- :488 computes `activeStateKey = createRouterCacheKey(activeSegment, true)`, and create-router-cache-key.js returns `${segment[0]}|${segment[1]}|${segment[2]}` for a dynamic segment → `id|1|d` vs `id|2|d`.
- :605 renders the segment as `jsxs(TemplateContext.Provider, {...}, stateKey)` — stateKey IS the React key, so a changed key unmounts the old subtree and mounts a new one.
- bfcache-state-manager.js:13 sets `MAX_BF_CACHE_ENTRIES = __NEXT_CACHE_COMPONENTS ? 3 : 1`, and web/next.config.ts does not enable `cacheComponents`, so the <Activity> state-preservation path is off entirely.

MEASURED, NOT JUST READ: I built a throwaway probe app in /tmp against this repo's own node_modules (Next 16.2.6, webpack dev, no cacheComponents) with an `[id]` page holding useState plus a module-level mount counter, and drove a client-side <Link> nav /p/1 → /p/2 with Playwright. Result: `sticky=DIRTY` reverted to `sticky=INITIAL`, instance went 2 → 3 (the module counter surviving proves it was a soft navigation, not a reload), and `document.contains(oldNode) === false`. Verdict: STATE RESET, component REMOUNTED. The probe dir is deleted; the repo was never written to (node_modules verified intact).

So all three claimed impacts fail:
1. The "deterministic repro" (visit a 404/403 id, then a valid id, see the stale error banner stacked above the new order) cannot happen — `error` is reinitialized to null on the fresh mount.
2. "loading is never reset to true, so order A's full detail view renders for the duration of B's request" cannot happen — `loading` reinitializes to true, so the skeleton at line 158 renders.
3. "order A's data can persist under order B's URL" cannot happen — instance A is unmounted (DOM node measured detached); its late setOrder is a no-op on an unmounted component and cannot reach instance B's state.

coverageGaps.gap: Expired or invalid JWTs return HTTP 403, but the web client only reacts to 401 — every logged-in user silently bricks at the 24h token expiry with no recovery path
coverageGaps.why: `SecurityConfig` (/Users/jadyn/Development/IYAE/server/src/main/java/com/iyae/config/SecurityConfig.java:29-57) configures no `exceptionHandling`/`authenticationEntryPoint` and registers no formLogin/httpBasic, so Spring Security falls back to `Http403ForbiddenEntryPoint` — the server's own tests confirm this (`SavedProductControllerTest`: "403 for each unauthenticated"). `JwtAuthenticationFilter.authenticate` (JwtAuthenticationFilter.java:45-60) returns silently without authenticating when the token is expired, the user row is missing, `ver < tokenVersion`, or email is unverified. Meanwhile /Users/jadyn/Development/IYAE/web/lib/api.ts:53 clears the token and redirects to /login ONLY on `res.status === 401`. Net effect: at the 24h expiry boundary (`app.jwt.expiration-ms` 86400000) every API call starts throwing `ApiError(403)`, the stale token is never cleared, the user is never sent to /login, and the app renders as a cascade of error banners forever. The same dead-end hits any user whose `tokenVersion` was bumped by a password reset and any unverified account. This is the single highest-volume production failure in the tree — it fires for 100% of users on a daily cadence — and neither web-auth, srv-security-config, srv-authz-matrix nor x-error-ux reported it.
coverageGaps.suggestedScope: web/lib/api.ts, server/.../config/SecurityConfig.java, server/.../security/JwtAuthenticationFilter.java

coverageGaps.gap: No production ADMIN account can exist, so the entire moderation and abuse-response surface is unreachable on a correctly-configured deploy
coverageGaps.why: `DataSeeder` is annotated `@Profile("!prod")` (/Users/jadyn/Development/IYAE/server/src/main/java/com/iyae/config/DataSeeder.java:22) and is the only thing that creates the ADMIN row (DataSeeder.java:93-100, comment: "granted only via seed/DB"). `AuthService.register` hard-rejects ADMIN (AuthService.java:86-89). There is no admin-provisioning endpoint, no CLI, no migration, and no instruction anywhere in `prod_deploy.sh`, `.env.example`, or the docs — a repo-wide grep for admin bootstrap turns up only test fixtures and PRP plans. So `docker-compose.prod.yml:36` (`SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: prod`) correctly suppresses the known-password seed account the audit flagged, and in doing so leaves the production database with zero ADMIN users. `/api/admin/**` is `hasRole("ADMIN")` (SecurityConfig.java:51), so `/admin`, the KPI dashboard, the post-report queue, comment removal and the durable `moderation_locked` takedown are all permanently inaccessible. The audit found the insecure-default half of this (the "!prod" deny-list) and missed that the secure path has no escape hatch. The only remediation is a hand-written SQL INSERT with a bcrypt hash, undocumented and unreviewed.
coverageGaps.suggestedScope: server/.../config/DataSeeder.java, server/.../service/AuthService.java, prod_deploy.sh, .env.example

coverageGaps.gap: No logout, no session revocation, and no way to suspend or ban a user — a compromised or abusive account cannot be stopped
coverageGaps.why: A repo-wide grep for `logout` across server/src/main/java returns nothing: there is no `/api/auth/logout` endpoint. `token_version` (V19 migration) is incremented in exactly one place — `AuthService.resetPassword` (AuthService.java:313). `JwtAuthenticationFilter.java:52` is the only consumer. So the web `logout()` merely deletes localStorage; the signed JWT remains valid for the rest of its 24h TTL on any device that captured it, and the only revocation mechanism in the product requires the victim to still control their mailbox. Separately, there is no account-state concept at all: no `enabled`/`status`/`suspended_at` column on users, no admin action in `AdminModerationService` that touches a user, and `JwtAuthenticationFilter.java:61-64` builds the principal with Spring's always-enabled `User` constructor. An admin (if one existed — see the ADMIN-bootstrap gap) can archive a post and resolve a report but cannot stop the account from immediately posting again. The audit covered UGC takedown mechanics and the report queue but never asked what happens to the offender, and treated JWT lifecycle only as a storage question (localStorage/CSP).
coverageGaps.suggestedScope: server/.../service/AuthService.java, server/.../security/JwtTokenProvider.java, server/.../service/AdminModerationService.java, server/.../entity/User.java

coverageGaps.gap: Community post images are unbounded base64 data URIs persisted directly into MySQL, with no size validation and no rate limit on post creation
coverageGaps.why: `LocalImagePicker` reads the chosen file with `FileReader.readAsDataURL` (/Users/jadyn/Development/IYAE/web/components/profile/LocalImagePicker.tsx:81,98), and `CreateFashionPostDialog.handleSubmit` puts that data URI straight into the server payload: `mediaUrls: selectedImage ? [selectedImage] : []` (CreateFashionPostDialog.tsx:210) then `await postsApi.create(payload)` (line 219). Server-side, `PostRequest.mediaUrls` is a bare `List<String>` with no `@Size` on the list and no length constraint on the elements (/Users/jadyn/Development/IYAE/server/src/main/java/com/iyae/dto/PostRequest.java:9), and `PostService.createPost` serialises it verbatim into `posts.media_urls JSON` (PostService.java:54,64; V8__community_tables.sql:8). `RateLimitFilter.RULES` has no rule for `/api/posts`, and nginx allows 20MB bodies (`nginx/nginx.conf:13 client_max_body_size 20m`). So each post can push ~20MB of base64 into the row, unlimited posts per user, on the same unreplicated volume the audit already found has no backup — and because the feed selects the column, a single page of 20 posts can return hundreds of MB, multiplying the N+1 findings into a bandwidth and heap problem. coverageGaps.gap: Production email sender defaults to Resend's shared sandbox address, which can only deliver to the account owner — and email deliverability (SPF/DKIM/DMARC, domain verification) was never audited as a class
coverageGaps.why: `docker-compose.prod.yml:93` sets `MAIL_FROM: ${RESEND_FROM_EMAIL:-onboarding@resend.dev}` and `.env.example:136` ships that same sandbox value as the default. `prod_deploy.sh` validates nothing about RESEND_* (grep for RESEND/MAIL in prod_deploy.sh: no matches). `web/app/api/internal/mail/send/route.ts:53` passes it to Resend unchanged. Resend permits `onboarding@resend.dev` to send only to the API-key owner's own verified address and rejects every other recipient — so on a deploy that sets `RESEND_API_KEY` but forgets `RESEND_FROM_EMAIL`, 100% of verification and password-reset emails fail. Both failure modes are swallowed by design: registration logs a warning and still succeeds, and forgot-password always returns 200 to prevent enumeration. Combined with `NEXT_PUBLIC_REQUIRE_EMAIL_VERIFICATION` being unreachable in a prod build (already found) and the filter's verification gate (JwtAuthenticationFilter.java:58), nobody can sign up and nobody can recover an account, with zero signal. Beyond the default: nothing in the repo documents domain verification, SPF, DKIM or a DMARC record, so even a correct `RESEND_FROM_EMAIL=noreply@iyae.ca` lands in spam. This whole risk class had no surface — web-internal-api audited the route's authz and payload handling, not whether mail arrives.
coverageGaps.suggestedScope: docker-compose.prod.yml, prod_deploy.sh, .env.example, web/app/api/internal/mail/send/route.ts, docs/

coverageGaps.gap: The money-path CRITICAL has no configuration surface to remediate it: STRIPE_SECRET_KEY and STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET appear in no env file, no compose file, and no deploy script
coverageGaps.why: A grep for `STRIPE` across `.env.example`, `docker-compose.yml`, `docker-compose.prod.yml`, `prod_deploy.sh` and `dev.sh` returns zero matches. `CheckoutService.java:53` reads `@Value("${STRIPE_SECRET_KEY:}")` with a blank default and branches to `stubCheckout` (line 78) / `stubResaleCheckout` (line 254), logging "STRIPE_SECRET_KEY not configured" at INFO (lines 314, 361). `docker-compose.prod.yml` (lines 23-42) enumerates every other secret the server needs — JWT, DB, AI keys, INTERNAL_MAIL_SECRET — and passes neither Stripe variable. coverageGaps.gap: No log rotation and no container hardening anywhere in the production stack — logs grow unbounded on the same unbacked-up disk as the database
coverageGaps.why: `docker-compose.prod.yml` (146 lines, read in full) contains no `logging:` key on any of its six services, so all five long-running containers use Docker's default `json-file` driver with no `max-size` or `max-file`. Those logs accumulate on the same host filesystem as the `mysql_data` and `assets_data` volumes, which the audit already established have no backup and no replication — and the stack has no restart policy, so the disk-full failure mode is a permanent outage of everything at once. Also absent from every service: `cap_drop`, `security_opt: [no-new-privileges:true]`, `read_only`, `user:`, `ulimits`, and `stop_grace_period` (the last one notable because the audit separately found no graceful shutdown in Spring and no SIGTERM handling in the worker — there is nothing on either side of that contract). The audit covered resource limits, restart policies, backups and the web container's root user individually; log retention and the container-escape/hardening posture of the compose file were not examined as classes.
coverageGaps.suggestedScope: docker-compose.prod.yml, server/Dockerfile, worker/Dockerfile.rigging

coverageGaps.gap: Zero CRITICAL findings on the auth path is a suspicious silence — here is the concrete re-examination list
coverageGaps.why: The money path has two CRITICALs and the PII path has three, but authentication produced only HIGHs and MEDIUMs (DataSeeder, auth-config, timing side-channel, missing verify/reset rate limits). Four specific things a follow-up must re-test, beyond the 403-vs-401 and revocation gaps above: (1) `JwtTokenProvider.generateToken(String email)` (JwtTokenProvider.java:26-28) hardcodes `ver=0`; both production call sites correctly pass `user.getTokenVersion()` (AuthService.java:158,178) so it is test-only dead code today, but any future caller would mint tokens that `JwtAuthenticationFilter.java:52` rejects on sight for every user who has ever reset a password — a silent, permanent, per-user lockout that no test would catch since `JwtTokenProviderTest` exercises the overload in isolation. Delete it. (2) There is no `@PreAuthorize`/`@Secured` anywhere in the server; the URL rules in SecurityConfig are the sole authorization layer, so any controller added at a path not matched by lines 35-51 silently inherits only `anyRequest().authenticated()` — the authz matrix is correct today and structurally fragile. (3) `/api/designer/**` is `hasRole("DESIGNER")` (line 49), which excludes ADMIN — worth confirming no admin workflow needs it. (4) Spring Security 6 filters the ERROR dispatch type by default, so an unauthenticated request that triggers the already-found never-logging catch-all 500 handler is re-authorized on the `/error` forward and surfaces as 403 — masking the outage twice over. Verify the real status code an anonymous 500 produces.
coverageGaps.suggestedScope: server/.../security/JwtTokenProvider.java, server/.../config/SecurityConfig.java, server/.../config/GlobalExceptionHandler.java

coverageGaps.gap: The next@16.2.6 CRITICAL asserts RCE/SSRF without naming a CVE or demonstrating that the vulnerable path is reachable in this configuration
coverageGaps.why: The finding title claims "multiple disclosed unauthenticated vulnerabilities including RCE and SSRF in the built-in Image Optimization API" but identifies no CVE, no affected-version range, and no fixed version — so the fix cannot be validated against the committed `web/package-lock.json`, and the upgrade target is unspecified for a framework the repo explicitly warns is full of breaking changes (`web/AGENTS.md`). The reachability assumption is also untested: `web/next.config.ts` (29 lines, read in full) declares no `images` block at all, so `images.remotePatterns` is empty and remote-URL optimization — the usual SSRF primitive — is off by default. `next/image` *is* used in 13 files, all against same-origin `/uploads/products/...` paths, so the chain that actually matters here is designer-uploaded bytes (whose type the audit's own advisory says is validated from the client-supplied Content-Type, not content) flowing into the local optimizer. That is a plausible and worse-than-stated story, but it is a different finding from the one written, with a different blast radius and a different mitigation (disable the optimizer / validate magic bytes / gate uploads) available if the upgrade is risky. A CRITICAL that drives a framework bump needs the CVE ids and the reachable-path proof written down.
coverageGaps.suggestedScope: web/package.json, web/package-lock.json, web/next.config.ts, server/.../service/FileStorageService.java

coverageGaps.gap: The authentication filter performs a database round trip on every single authenticated request, uncached, with no connection-pool sizing configured
coverageGaps.why: `JwtAuthenticationFilter.authenticate` calls `userRepository.findByEmail(email)` (JwtAuthenticationFilter.java:47) on every request bearing a Bearer token, purely to read `tokenVersion`, `emailVerified` and `role` — three values that could ride in the JWT claims (`ver` already does). This is the hottest code path in the application: every cart read, every poll of `useGenerationStatus`/`useRiggingStatus`/`useOutfitRiggingStatus` (3s intervals), every `useWeather` poll and every feed page pays an extra query before any business logic runs. It compounds directly with two findings the audit already has — "no connection-pool, thread-pool or container resource sizing in production" and the community-feed N+1 — because the pool exhaustion those cause is reached sooner when each request needs one more connection-turn, and the resulting 500s hit the never-logging catch-all handler. x-perf examined catalog LIKE scans, KPI table scans, missing indexes and worker serialization, but not the per-request auth cost.
coverageGaps.suggestedScope: server/.../security/JwtAuthenticationFilter.java, server/src/main/resources/application-prod.yml
